# AI Surfaces: chatbot & deskbot

The AI subsystem serves **two product surfaces** through **one orchestrator**. They are told apart by an explicit `surface` discriminant — not by implicit request-flag truthiness.

## The two surfaces

| | **chatbot** | **deskbot** |
|---|---|---|
| **Role** | The v10r **expert** — *why* and *how* the project is built | The in-desk **operator** — does anything a user can do via the desk UI |
| **Mode** | Read-only, grounded, citation-faithful Q&A | Agentic, mutating, approval-gated |
| **Route** | `POST /api/ai/chatbot` | `POST /api/ai/deskbot` |
| **Client** | `composites/chatbot/Chatbot.svelte` — persistent, minimizable, non-modal panel; live thread owned by the `chatbot-session` singleton (see [../app-shell/ai-assistant.md](../app-shell/ai-assistant.md)) | `chat/ChatPanel.svelte` (desk panel) |
| **Profile** | `CHATBOT_PROFILE` (`ai/profile/chatbot.ts`) — capabilities: completion · project-map · project-docs · catalog · navigation · pattern-library · site-awareness · compaction | `DESKBOT_PROFILE` (`ai/profile/deskbot.ts`) — capabilities: completion · desk-awareness · desk-files · desk-edit · desk-create · desk-delete · desk-ask · desk-plan · compaction |
| **Harness** | the chatbot capabilities' tools → `chatbotToolMeta` | the scoped desk capabilities' tools → `deskbotToolMeta` |
| **Tools** | `search_catalog`, `search_project_docs`, `search_pattern_library` (3) | `desk_*` read/write/create/delete, `desk_search_knowledge`, `desk_propose_plan` (14) — zero overlap with the chatbot set. (`resolve_ref` mounts on both harnesses but is compaction infra, deliberately outside `TOOL_MANIFEST`.) |
| **System prompt** | Vely's identity + the capabilities' guidance + `<project-overview>`/`<catalog-map>` ‖ `<current-page>` + retrieved context + guides — composed by `composeTurn` ([profiles.md](./profiles.md)) | the operator's identity + the granted capabilities' guidance ‖ `<permissions>` + workspace + `<desk-context>` + `<desk-layout>` + `<planning>` on demand — same composer |
| **Corpus (retrieval)** | System-owned (`source IN docs,catalog`, `SYSTEM_DOCS_USER_ID`) — curated, static (catalog slice graph-seeded; docs-corpus graph tier dormant) | The user's **own** desk files — per-user, mutable, not graph-seeded, private |
| **Location-awareness** | **site-awareness** — the current public route as a thin server-resolved page label (public-catalog only); _v1 built (dev, uncommitted), see [site-awareness.md](./site-awareness.md)_ | **desk-awareness** — live desk state (`panelContext`/`deskLayout`/`activeWorkspace`): which panels & files are open; _live_ |
| **Invariants** | Never emits a `DeskEffect`; never creates a proposal | All mutations route through `db/desk`; write & destructive tools require human approval (proposal → approve-route), never mutating in-loop; only reversible creates run in-loop |

(A third `rag-demo` value once drove the showcase retrieval-pipeline demo; it was retired 2026-08 when the architecture pages at `/showcases/ai/chatbot` + `/showcases/ai/deskbot` absorbed the retrieval pedagogy — `TurnSurface` is a closed two-member union again.)

## Dispatch — the `surface` discriminant

`ChatInput.surface: TurnSurface` (`'chatbot' | 'deskbot'`) is the single named dispatch decision in `chat-orchestrator.ts`. The two per-surface routes set it explicitly — it is a **required** field, never derived from request flags (the legacy `useLlmwiki`/`useRetrieval` derivation was removed with the rag-demo surface):

| Route | Surface |
|---|---|
| `POST /api/ai/chatbot` | `orchestrateChat({ surface: 'chatbot' })` |
| `POST /api/ai/deskbot` | `orchestrateChat({ surface: 'deskbot' })` |

Both share one entry guard, `guardAiRequest()` (`guard.ts`), which dedups auth → `aiConfigured` → (rate-limit ∥ daily-budget — two independent Redis reads issued together, the rate-limit answer taking precedence when both deny) so the routes stay thin and the rate-limit key can't drift across copies. The chatbot surface additionally requires a *fresh user turn*; any other turn takes the plain deskbot streaming path. There is no "resume after approval" turn any more: an approved plan's outcome reaches the model as the **execution receipt message** the approve door persists (see the one-door rule), so no model call follows an approval and a failed plan cannot fall through into a mutating turn.

```
orchestrateChatInner → resolve surface →
  surface === 'chatbot'  → corpus-map-anchored grounded turn (+ relevance-gated docs prefetch)
  surface === 'deskbot'  → agentic desk tool loop (default; also takes any non-fresh turn)
```

## Harness split (zero tool overlap)

The two tool collections are **physically and semantically disjoint** and grow independently:

- `chatbotToolMeta` — read-only retrieval tools. **No `scope` field** (uses surface-neutral `ToolMeta`/`ToolRisk`).
- `deskbotToolMeta` — desk CRUD/action tools, each carrying its gating `DeskToolScope` (`DeskToolMeta`).
- `allToolMeta` — the union, for admin/telemetry that needs every tool regardless of surface.

Every tool also declares its `executor`. All chatbot tools and all deskbot data tools are `server`; the deskbot's three workspace tools (`desk:arrange`) are `client` — **client actions**, run by the browser that sent the turn and never able to change stored data ([agent-actions.md](./agent-actions.md)).

A chatbot tool never carries a desk scope; a deskbot tool always does. The `/admin/ai/tools` topology view derives branch from membership (`name in chatbotToolMeta`), not from a scope artifact.

## One-door rule (deskbot mutations)

Every deskbot mutation flows through the single SSOT `executeDeskToolCall()` (`tools/desk-execute.ts`) — the **one door** — the in-loop creates included. **Write and destructive** tools never mutate in the agent loop: their `execute` reads the target and returns a `requiresApproval` sentinel carrying the **reviewed baseline** (`ProposedTarget`: file id, kind, name, `version`, `updatedAt`), which the orchestrator turns into a pending `agent_proposal` (a PlanCard). `desk_propose_plan` does the same for a whole sequence after `validateProposedPlan` (`proposals/plan-validation.ts`) has checked every step against the door it will go through: a known mutation tool, args that parse against the tool's contract (`DESK_MUTATION_INPUTS`, the one valibot schema per tool that also produces the model-facing JSON Schema), an owned target of the right kind. Risk and recovery wording on the card are derived from the tool, never model-authored. The step that asked for approval is the turn's last (`stoppedAtApproval` in `stopWhen`) — the **approval boundary** — so a turn has exactly one proposal and no "awaiting approval" prose behind it.

The mutation runs **only** via `POST /api/ai/proposals/[id]/approve` → `executeProposal` (`proposals/execute-proposal.ts`), which records a real `approvedBy`/`approvedAt` and, per step, writes a **step receipt** (`ai.agent_proposal_step`) INSIDE the transaction that runs the step's mutation: a mutation and its receipt commit or roll back together, the receipts' primary key refuses a second execution of a step, and after a crash the completed set is exactly the receipts (a row still `executing` past its lease heals to `failed('interrupted')` on the next read). The door re-parses the persisted args and compares the reviewed baseline — `expectedVersion` for cell and markdown writes, `updatedAt` for rename and delete — so a file that moved on since review is a `conflict` receipt, never a silent overwrite. The plan is a sequence: it stops at the first non-`ok` step and the earlier steps stay (no rollback), which the receipts say. Reversible **creates** (soft-delete-recoverable) mutate in-loop, auto-approved, through the same door.

A plan that ran can be **undone** once: `POST /api/ai/proposals/[id]/revert` → `revertProposal` (`proposals/revert-proposal.ts`). Every `ok` step wrote a **recovery point** on its receipt (`agent_proposal_step.recovery`, server-only): the state it left the file in and what puts it back (a pre-image revision id, the previous name, the deletion time, the created file). The revert claims `revert_status` from null — one undo per proposal, and the claim itself requires the caller to own the conversation, so no door can spend another user's undo — refuses a plan whose steps recorded no recovery point (they ran before undo existed), walks the receipts in reverse, and runs one compensating desk mutation per step in its own transaction with a **revert receipt** (`agent_proposal_revert_step`, keyed by the forward step it undoes) behind the same fence and heartbeat as the run. Each undo is a compare-and-swap against what the plan left behind, chained per file; a file the user touched since is a `conflict`, left as it is and named in the deterministic revert message, while the other files are still undone. A revert whose process died is healed to `revert_failed` by the next status read (`GET /api/ai/proposals/[id]`), and only the client's own request in flight holds the desk bot busy. Compensation, not rollback: there is no all-or-nothing claim. The restores go to the desk domain directly as the asking user — they never pass through `executeDeskToolCall`, so the model's tool surface is unchanged.

What the user reads afterwards is deterministic: `executeProposal` persists an **execution receipt message** (one assistant row: "Ran the approved plan (2 of 3 steps) … 2. Rename — conflict …") and answers with the `ProposalOutcome` (`#lib/types/ai-proposal`: status, receipts, the `DeskEffect[]` of the completed steps derived by `effectsForStep`, the receipt message). The desk-bot session (`panels/bot/desk-bot-session.svelte.ts`) moves the card's **proposal run** through `approving` to that status, dispatches the effects — a `desk:refresh_file` reloads the open sheet or document, which answers `ai:file_refreshed` so the I/O log records what the panel now shows — and puts the receipt message into the thread, where the model reads it as history on the next user turn. `GET /api/ai/proposals/[id]` answers the same outcome for a lost response, a 409 or a remount; the run is `unknown` until it does.

Three tests guard distinct properties of the door. `index.test.ts` drift-guards tool *name* coverage — it fails if a mutating deskbot tool lacks a replay case, a scope, a recovery or an input schema, so the replay path can never silently fall behind the live tool set. `desk-execute.test.ts` guards the contract — empty args are refused by the schema before any read, a missing baseline refuses an update/rename/delete, a moved-on file is a `conflict`. `execute-proposal.pglite.test.ts` guards the receipts — a step whose receipt cannot be written rolls back with it, a receipted step is never run twice. `revert-proposal.pglite.test.ts` guards the undo — every step kind is put back, a file edited after the plan is left alone as a conflict, an undo runs once, another user's undo reaches none of the files.

## Retrieval: one shared kernel, two profiles, two corpora

The subsystem is called **retrieval** everywhere — `server/retrieval/`, `/api/retrieval/*`, the `retrieval` pgSchema and `/admin/ai/retrieval`. It spans the chunk engine, the ingest door and the corpus map (`retrieval.corpus_map`, the ingest-built map of a collection's corpus), so a definition naming only the engine is incomplete. The informal umbrella "retrieval" was retired in favour of the one word the code uses.

The retrieval **engine** (`retrieval/retrieve()` — embed → tiers → RRF fusion, with the single `user_id` tenant-isolation filter) is **shared mechanism**. The two surfaces exercise it as distinct **profiles**:

| | chatbot profile | deskbot profile |
|---|---|---|
| Corpus | `SYSTEM_DOCS_USER_ID` (docs/catalog) | The user's own desk files |
| Tiers | Designed 1–3 (graph tier valuable — catalog is Neo4j-seeded); **live: the chatbot requests tier-1 only** — tiers 2–3 unexercised by the chatbot today | 1–2 (no graph — desk files aren't graph-seeded) |
| Grounding | Injected `<project-overview>` corpus map + relevance-gated docs prefetch + catalog grounding; post-stream path verification | `desk:ask` read-only tool (`desk_search_knowledge`); no citation chips. Read-only: excluded from `hasMutatingScope`/the desk step budget/the plan gate — it never triggers plan-before-execute (only the turn's mutating tools do) |
| Freshness | Static curated corpus | Mutable — `aiContext` opt-in; reconciled off the hot path by the `desk-retrieval-sync` job (polls `updatedAt`), not on each save |

The kernel is never forked (a duplicated `user_id` filter would be a cross-tenant-leak risk); the corpus boundary is purely `document.userId`.

## Context assembly — one door: the profile

Everything that decides what enters a surface's system prompt and tool set lives in its **profile** ([profiles.md](./profiles.md)): the identity, and one capability per thing the assistant can do — its tools, its when-to-use guidance, the rule that activates it, its grounding lane, its on-demand guide, its verifier. `composeTurn(profile, turn, recorder)` (`ai/profile/profile.ts`) runs the capabilities' rules, the grounding lanes in parallel under one shared query embedding, assembles the prompt block by block in cache order (identity → guidance → stable grounding ‖ awareness → dynamic grounding → guides), mounts the active capabilities' tools and hands back the step budget — and records every decision on the turn trace. The chatbot's gates are its capabilities' rules: the triviality gate (`project-docs`), the deixis gate (`site-awareness`), the navigation gate (`navigation`); the deskbot's plan rule is `desk-plan`'s, its `<permissions>` block is rendered from the scoped capabilities × the granted scopes (`desk-awareness`).

Nothing runs the pre-generation half a second time: the "Turn inspector" section of `/showcases/ai/chatbot` (`#orchestration`) opens a **persisted** turn — the committed fixture signed-out, any of the viewer's own turns signed in — and shows what the profile made available, what the lanes considered, what entered each model call, what ran and what was cited ([turn-trace.md](./turn-trace.md)). `GET /api/ai/profiles/[surface]` answers the profile itself — identity text, capabilities with guidance and tool schemas, grounding inventory — for a signed-in viewer; it is the inspector's AVAILABLE side.

## Location-awareness — two profiles

Each surface knows **where the user currently is**, so deixis ("this", "here") resolves to their actual location. This is **location-awareness** — one idea, two surface-specific profiles:

- **site-awareness** (chatbot) — Vely's awareness of the public route you're viewing, as a thin server-resolved page label (public-catalog routes only, never the raw path or DOM). *v1 built (dev, uncommitted) — see [site-awareness.md](./site-awareness.md).*
- **desk-awareness** (deskbot) — the deskbot's awareness of your live desk state: which panels and files are open (`panelContext`/`deskLayout`/`activeWorkspace`), first-party and mutable. *Live.*

**Same concept, different depth.** Site-awareness and desk-awareness are two profiles of one idea — ground the user's *here*/*this* in their current location — at deliberately unequal depth. Desk-awareness is rich, first-party, and mutable (full panel and file content); site-awareness is intentionally thin — a single server-resolved route label, public-catalog routes only, never DOM-scraped. The asymmetry is **by design, not a parity gap**: deeper page extraction (DOM, selected text) is a standing security finding, not missing work.

The **mechanism** behind site-awareness is **page-awareness** — resolving `page.route.id` to a `<current-page>` label. "Location-awareness" is the family, "site-awareness"/"desk-awareness" the two profiles, and "page-awareness" the chatbot-side mechanism. Full design: [site-awareness.md](./site-awareness.md).

## Status

**Live:** the naming + dispatch discriminant; the **per-surface route split** (`/api/ai/chatbot` · `/api/ai/deskbot`) behind the shared `guardAiRequest`; the harness split (zero overlap); the one-door rule (validated plans, reviewed baselines, step receipts in the mutation's transaction, deterministic execution receipt message, no resume turn — approval binds execution); the **tool-layer approval gate** (every write/overwrite/delete — even single-target — returns a `requiresApproval` sentinel and mutates only through a human-approved proposal recorded with `approvedBy`/`approvedAt`; the model-minted `confirmed` self-handshake is gone; `shouldRequirePlan` widened to `mutatingScopeGranted && destructiveIntent`, now soft planning guidance; a pre-image `desk.file_revision` snapshot makes an approved overwrite/delete recoverable); the `surface` analytics column (`ai_surface` enum on `ai.conversation` + `ai.model_call`, stamped at creation, `model_call_surface_idx`); the chatbot retrieval profile (relevance-gated system-docs prefetch); and the **deskbot retrieval profile** — `desk:ask` read-only grounding tool (`desk_search_knowledge`) over the user's own `aiContext` desk files, ingested via the shared kernel (`source = 'desk'`) and kept fresh by the `desk-retrieval-sync` job (polls `desk.file.updatedAt`).

**Browser-verified 2026-06-25:** the chatbot's Phase-C foundation grounding is live — an injected `<project-overview>` corpus map (today `loadProjectMap()` → `getCorpusMap([SYSTEM_DOCS_USER_ID], PROJECT_DOCS_COLLECTION_ID)`) plus **tier-1-only** retrieval. The anchor is the load-bearing fix for the original broad-question bug: "how do I use v10r?" now answers correctly with real `/docs/...` citations (5/5 functional probes green). Hierarchical docs chunking landed too, but is groundwork for future tier-2 surfaces — it does not change chatbot answers today, and the corpus conversion is partial (36/93 docs, quota-gated). See [knowledge-base.md](./knowledge-base.md#wired-vs-scaffold-the-honest-map).

**Built 2026-09-12:** the per-surface **profiles** (`ai/profile/`, `ai/capabilities/`; [profiles.md](./profiles.md)) — identity + capabilities composed per turn, one owner per rule, Vely's own identity. **Planned:** the physical `_shared`/`chatbot`/`deskbot` directory layout — both surfaces still dispatch from one `chat-orchestrator.ts`. Also planned: a DB `ai_tool` registry behind the declarative `TOOL_MANIFEST`. **Site-awareness** — the chatbot's [location-awareness](#location-awareness--two-profiles) profile ([site-awareness.md](./site-awareness.md)) — is built and live; its sibling **desk-awareness** ships as the deskbot's `panelContext`/`deskLayout` injection.
files.docs/blueprint/ai/untrusted-content.md: # Untrusted content How v10r keeps a document a user ingested from steering the assistant that reads it — the "lethal trifecta" of prompt injection, and the code that holds each of its three legs. ## Untrusted-content boundary **Problem.** An assistant that (1) reads content someone else could have written, (2) can reach private data, and (3) can send something out — a fetch, an email, an image URL in its answer — can be made to exfiltrate that data by instructions hidden in the content. No detector reliably spots the instructions; the defence that holds is structural: bound the content, and take away a leg. The deskbot meets leg 1 on every turn — open panels, file reads and knowledge search are all user-controlled text, file names included. **Method.** One rule per leg, each enforced in one place: | Leg | Rule | Where | |---|---|---| | 1. Untrusted input | Every tool declares `resultOrigin` (`system` · `user`). A `user` result reaches the model as one escaped `` element — through AI SDK `toModelOutput`, so the loop's own value (approval sentinels, desk effects, the turn trace) stays raw. Results replayed from earlier turns get the same wrapping, failing closed on any shape (a compacted projection, an error, a multi-part output). Prompt blocks (``, ``) were already escaped | `ai/untrusted-content.ts` (`withUntrustedBoundary` in `composeTurn`, `boundHistoryToolResults` in the orchestrator); `TOOL_MANIFEST` in `types/ai-tools.ts` | | 2. Exfiltration | Every tool declares `reach` (`internal` · `external`). An `external` tool must be approval-gated (`requiresApproval(risk)`). None exists today; because the label is self-declared, the gate also scans the tool modules and fails on a fetch, socket or delivery-channel import while every tool says `internal` | `untrusted-content.gate.test.ts` | | 3. Output channel | Model output renders with no `` (the automatic beacon) and no link to a host outside `TRUSTED_LINK_HOSTS`; only `http`/`https` | `utils/markdown.ts` (`untrusted: true` is the default) | The data-not-instructions rule (`profile/shared-rules.ts`) names the tag, so the model is told what the boundary means. That sentence is guidance; the escaping is the guarantee. **What is not claimed.** An error the AI SDK raises while running a tool (invalid input) reaches the model as its own `error-text`, outside the boundary; it echoes model-produced input, not stored content. Whether a model obeys text inside the boundary is not testable and not tested. Injection detectors and classifiers are not used: they are probabilistic, and a missed detection on a turn with all three legs is the whole incident. **Invariants.** - Every manifest tool declares `resultOrigin` and `reach`; a tool nobody declared is `user`. - No `user`-origin result reaches the model unescaped, in the turn that ran it or a later one. - No tool with `reach: 'external'` runs without a human-approved proposal. - Model output renders no image and no link to an unlisted host. **Client actions.** A tool the browser executes ([agent-actions.md](./agent-actions.md)) is `user` origin by construction: its result arrives in the request body. It is read through `parseClientActionResult` first — a bounded status, code, message and flat facts, anything else replaced by `malformed_result` — and then wrapped like every other replayed `user` result. **Adding a tool.** Declare `resultOrigin` honestly — anything that echoes user text, even a name, is `user`. A tool that sends anything outside the deployment is `external` and must be `write` or `destructive` risk, so it goes through the approval gate. **Do not use** the wrapper as the only defence on a surface that also has an unapproved `external` tool: wrapping lowers the odds, removing a leg removes the attack. Related: [threat-model.md](../security/threat-model.md) (the ingested-document adversary), [harness-lens.md](./harness-lens.md) (the approval gate).

# How Architecture Engineering works

Architecture Engineering turns what is known about a workload into explained architectural
decisions, an editable architecture model, and static checks. Everything below is
deterministic: ordered rules over a closed vocabulary. There are no weights, no scores and
no LLM, so the same input and engine revision always give the same output, and every output
says why.

Code: `pattern-library/architecture-engineering/` (framework-free and dependency-free, so the
stdio MCP server can run it under bare Bun). UI: `/studio/architecture`. MCP:
`explore_architecture`, `check_architecture`. Registry: `architecture-engineering`.

## The five domains

| Domain | Question | Decision records |
|---|---|---|
| Execution | Where and in which runtime does the work run? | `compute-placement`, `compute-runtime` |
| Communication | How do the parts talk? | `interaction-style` |
| Data | Where does data live and where is it processed? | `data-store`, `processing-locality` |
| Deployment | How many deployable units, and which shape? | `deployment-shape` |
| Performance | What do we do when it is too slow? | `compute-acceleration` |

## Decision records

A decision record (`decision-record.ts`, catalogue `decisions.json`) is an ADR made
executable: identity and revision, the problem, the alternatives (each with benefits,
drawbacks, `prefer_when`, contraindications and pattern ids), **ordered rules**
(`when` → `choose`, with `because`), a fallback, what would make you revisit it, the evidence
(each item carries its kind), migrations between alternatives, and how to confirm the choice.

`parseDecisionCatalog` validates the catalogue when it is imported; `patterns:validate` checks
that every pattern id resolves in the registry and every evidence reference exists (a route,
an app route, or a file with its anchor).

### Why ordered rules and not a score

A weighted matrix hides its reasoning in the weights, and two matrices disagree for reasons
nobody can read. An ordered rule table says exactly which fact decided, and a reviewer can
argue with one rule. The order encodes priority: a hard constraint (offline, sensitive data
that must not leave the device) is written before a preference.

### How a rule is evaluated

For each decision, rules are tried in order (`explore.ts`):

1. A rule whose every condition matches a **known** factor value **fires**. Its alternative is
   chosen with `basis: 'rule'`, and the inputs it used are listed.
2. A rule blocked only by **unknown** factors does not fire. It becomes **missing
   information**: "if these factors were known, this could become X".
3. A rule contradicted by a known value is recorded on the alternative as `contradicted_by`
   (which factor, its value, what the rule needed).
4. With no firing rule, the **fallback**, always the simplest alternative, is chosen with
   `basis: 'fallback'` and labelled a default.

Every alternative not chosen therefore carries a reason: contradicted, reachable with more
information, or outranked by an earlier rule. Unknown stays unknown; nothing is inferred.

### Evidence kinds

`measured` (with its conditions) · `live-measurement` (run on your device, not recorded) ·
`reference-implementation` · `documented-reasoning` · `external-study` · `estimate`. The
Studio shows the kind next to every claim. **Evidence labs** (`evidence-labs.ts`) link the
existing v10r experiments (`/showcases/wasm`, `/showcases/external-service`) and state the gap
where none exists: application vs database processing has no v10r measurement yet, so that
decision rests on documented reasoning and says so.

## The architecture model

`architecture-model.ts`: zones (trust or runtime boundaries), components (`ArchitectureNode`,
one of twelve `NodeKind`s, each with allowed placements, accepted protocols and
infrastructure requirements), connections (protocol, sync/async, data flow, authentication,
failure handling), and constraints. Positions live apart, in `ArchitectureLayout`, after
the C4/Structurizr split of model and view: moving a box never changes the architecture, and
an exported file (`ArchitectureFile`) round-trips byte-stably through
`stringifyArchitectureFile`.

The model is **untrusted input** wherever it comes from (import, local storage, MCP):
`parseArchitectureModel` is strict (unknown keys refused, not dropped), bounded
(`MODEL_LIMITS`), checks integrity (unique ids, no dangling references, placements allowed for
the kind), and fails closed. Nothing in a model is executed or rendered as HTML.

Edits go through `model-operations.ts`: each returns a new model or a named refusal
(`connection.self`, `placement.not-allowed`, `zone.in-use`, …), the same convention as
product composition. Explore → Design builds a starting model from a recommendation
(`model-from-recommendation.ts`).

## Static checks

`checks.ts` returns `ArchitectureFinding`s, each with a fixed severity per code, a category,
what was detected, why it matters, the constraint, a fix and patterns. Severities: `error` (a
stated fact contradicts a rule, e.g. a secret on a browser component), `warning` (usually a
problem), `unknown` (the model leaves a decisive property unstated), `recommendation` (a
simpler or safer option exists). **Security** is its own category and is checked by
`checkSecurity`, apart from runtime, communication, data and structure (`checkDesign`), so a
cosmetic check can never mask or downgrade it. Failure-handling checks apply only across
service boundaries; a plain database call is not flagged.

## Comparison and evolution

`compareArchitectures(baseline, variant)` diffs components, placements, connections, zones
and infrastructure requirements, counts deployment units, managed dependencies, network
connections and trust-boundary crossings, and lists findings introduced and resolved. Its
assessment is **qualitative** (`basis: 'qualitative'`): it says "one more synchronous network
call", never a number of milliseconds, and a test enforces that. A **variant**
(`deriveVariant`) records its baseline and the reason for the change; the evolution example
walks a monolith → background worker → Rust service → client compute.

## Studio

`/studio/architecture` lists the principles, the decision records and the labs. Its three
modes share one state (`_state/architecture-studio.svelte.ts`) under the area's layout, so
moving between them keeps every edit:

- **Explore** — factor selects (unknown first), ten example workloads, the explained
  recommendation, transfer to Design.
- **Design** — the canvas (xyflow, loaded lazily through `FlowDiagram`), plus a keyboard path
  through component and connection lists and inspectors; undo/redo with typing coalesced;
  local drafts; JSON import/export through the parser.
- **Engineer** — findings grouped by category, the decisions behind the model, variants with
  their reason, and the comparison.

Drafts are local-first (`localStorage`, labelled as such); the file format is the contract, so
a server store can come later without changing the model.

## Limits

- The catalogue is seven decisions; it covers the choices v10r itself has evidence for.
- Checks read structure and stated facts; they do not measure. A clean model is not a fast one.
- Comparison is qualitative. Numbers belong to labs, cited as evidence with their conditions.
- Decision content is English, like the registry; the Studio chrome is localized.

## 4. Architecture and data contracts

### 4.1 Where the code lives

`pattern-library/architecture-engineering/` — framework-free, dependency-free TypeScript
plus one JSON catalogue. It sits beside the registry because the stdio MCP server (bare
Bun, no `node_modules`) must import it by relative path, exactly like `query.ts`; the app

`vitest.config.ts` includes `pattern-library/**/*.test.ts`.

| File | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `vocabulary.ts` | Closed vocabularies: engineering domains, workload factors and their values, node kinds (default placement, allowed placements, `requires`), placements, protocols, zone kinds, evidence kinds |
| `decisions.json` | The decision catalogue (data) |
| `decision-record.ts` | Decision record types and fail-closed parse; pattern-id resolution |
| `explore.ts` | The decision engine: workload profile → recommendation per decision |
| `workload-examples.ts` | The ten Explore examples (profiles, not recommendations — the engine derives those) |
| `architecture-model.ts` | Architecture model + layout types, fail-closed parse of untrusted JSON, canonical stringify |

| `checks.ts` | Engineering checks: model → `ArchitectureFinding[]` |
| `compare.ts` | Two models → structured differences + qualitative assessment |

### 4.2 Decision record (`decisions.json`, `ARCHITECTURE_DECISION_FORMAT = 1`)

```ts
interface ArchitectureDecision {
  id: string;                       // kebab-case, stable
  revision: number;                 // bumps when rules or recommendation change
  domain: 'execution' | 'communication' | 'data' | 'deployment' | 'performance';
  title: string; question: string; description: string;
  problem: { workload: string; functional: string[]; nonfunctional: string[]; constraints: string[]; assumptions: string[] };
  alternatives: {
    id: string; approach: string; placement?: Placement; technologies: string[];
    benefits: string[]; drawbacks: string[]; prerequisites: string[]; contraindications: string[];
    patterns: string[];             // registry ids — must resolve
  }[];
  rules: { id: string; when: Partial<Record<WorkloadFactor, string[]>>; choose: string; because: string }[];
  fallback: { choose: string; because: string };   // the simplest alternative
  rejected: Record<string, string>; // why each non-default alternative loses by default
  changes_when: string[];           // conditions that flip the recommendation
  evidence: { kind: EvidenceKind; ref: string; claim: string; conditions?: string; limitations: string }[];
  evolution: { revisit_when: string[]; migrations: { from: string; to: string; path: string; implications: string }[] };
  confirmation?: string;            // how compliance is checked (MADR "confirmation")
}
type EvidenceKind = 'measured' | 'live-measurement' | 'reference-implementation' | 'documented-reasoning' | 'external-study' | 'estimate';
```

Evidence follows the *evidence status dimensions* discipline: kind, conditions and
limitations are separate fields; there is no score. `measured` requires `conditions`.

### 4.3 Decision engine (`explore.ts`)

Input: a `WorkloadProfile` — every factor is a closed value **or `unknown`**:
`workload`, `duration`, `dataVolume`, `dataOrigin`, `sensitivity`, `offline`, `latency`,
`compute`, `background`, `infrastructure`, `complexityTolerance`.

Per decision, rules are evaluated **in order**:

- a rule whose every named factor is known and matching **fires** → its alternative is
  chosen, its `because` recorded;
- a rule that could match but names an `unknown` factor is **undecided** → recorded as
  *missing information*: "if `background` were `required`, this would choose
  `background-job`";
- a rule contradicted by a known value is skipped;
- no rule fires → `fallback` (always the simplest alternative), flagged as a default.

Output (`ArchitectureRecommendation`): engine revision, the input profile echoed, and per
relevant decision: chosen alternative, fired rule id + reason, every other alternative
with its rejection reason, undecided rules (missing information), `changes_when`, evidence.
Same inputs + same catalogue revision ⇒ byte-identical output. No scores, no AI.

### 4.4 Architecture model (`ARCHITECTURE_MODEL_FORMAT = 1`)

```ts
interface ArchitectureModel {
  format: 1; id: string; name: string; description: string;
  derived_from?: string;            // the baseline a variant was duplicated from
  change_reason?: string;           // why this variant exists (evolution record)
  zones: { id: string; label: string; kind: 'client' | 'application' | 'data' | 'third-party' }[];
  nodes: {
    id: string; kind: NodeKind; label: string; zone: string;
    placement: Placement; responsibilities: string[];
    traits: { holds_secrets: boolean; cpu_intensive: boolean; long_running: boolean; stateful: boolean };
    decisions: string[]; patterns: string[];
  }[];
  connections: {
    id: string; from: string; to: string; protocol: Protocol; mode: 'sync' | 'async';
    data_flow: string;
    authenticated: 'yes' | 'no' | 'unknown';
    failure_handling: 'unknown' | 'none' | 'timeout' | 'retry' | 'timeout-and-retry' | 'queue-redelivery';
  }[];
  constraints: string[];
}
interface ArchitectureLayout { format: 1; positions: Record<string, { x: number; y: number }> }
```

Node kinds (12): `browser-app`, `browser-worker`, `wasm-module`, `app-server`,
`api-endpoint`, `background-worker`, `compute-service`, `relational-db`, `graph-db`,
`cache`, `object-storage`, `external-service`. Each declares allowed placements, a default,
and `requires` (from `PATTERN_REQUIREMENTS`).

The diagram is a projection: positions live only in `ArchitectureLayout`. Parsing treats
input as untrusted: strict objects, bounded sizes (nodes ≤ 200, strings ≤ 2 000 chars),
kebab-case ids, duplicate ids refused, dangling references refused, unknown format refused.
Nothing in a model is ever executed or rendered as HTML.

### 4.5 Engineering checks (`checks.ts`)

`checkArchitecture(model) → ArchitectureFinding[]`, each `{ code, severity, category,
subject, why, constraint, fix, patterns }`. Severities: `error` (a stated fact is
contradicted — e.g. a secret on a browser node), `warning` (a heuristic that usually
signals a problem), `recommendation` (simpler or safer option exists), `unknown` (the model
leaves a decisive property unstated). Categories keep **security** separate from
**runtime**, **communication**, **data** and **structure**. Initial codes:

| Code | Severity | Category |
|---|---|---|
| `secret.client-exposed` | error | security |
| `boundary.unauthenticated` | error | security |
| `boundary.auth-unknown` | unknown | security |
| `client.direct-data-access` | error | security |
| `main-thread.cpu` | warning | runtime |
| `request.long-running` | warning | runtime |
| `runtime.unsupported` | error | runtime |
| `protocol.incompatible` | error | communication |
| `boundary.failure-unknown` | unknown | communication |
| `boundary.no-failure-handling` | warning | communication |
| `boundary.unjustified-service` | recommendation | structure |
| `data.shared-ownership` | warning | data |
| `node.isolated` | recommendation | structure |

No check measures anything; none may claim performance numbers.

### 4.6 Comparison (`compare.ts`)

Two models → added/removed/changed nodes (by id), placement changes, connection changes,
zone changes, deployment units (distinct runtimes that must be deployed), network
boundaries crossed, synchronous network hops, operational requirements (union of node
`requires`, diffed), findings diff. Latency and complexity are reported as **qualitative**
statements labelled *qualitative — not measured*, with links to evidence where it exists.

### 4.7 Persistence

Local-first: `localStorage`, one index key plus one key per draft, labelled in the UI as
"saved in this browser only". Draft = `{ model, layout, savedAt }`. Export/import is one
JSON file `{ model, layout? }` parsed by the same fail-closed parser. No database schema,
no auth dependency. The model contract is storage-agnostic, so a server store can be added
later without touching it.

# Agent Experience (AX)

How v10r serves AI agents as first-class consumers: a machine-readable docs layer, an agent-facing URL map, self-correcting MCP errors, and a loopable convention checker.

v10r's consumption model *is* agent-mediated — the PRD's thesis is that an AI agent reads these tested patterns and adapts them to a new project. So agent experience here is not a feature bolted onto a human product; it is the delivery mechanism for the product itself. This document describes the four AX surfaces, the contracts they keep, and the constraints that shaped them.

---

## The four surfaces

| Surface | Consumer | Mechanism |
|---------|----------|-----------|
| `.md` docs layer | any HTTP agent (Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenCode send `Accept: text/markdown` today) | every published `/docs/**` page serves raw markdown at its URL + `.md`; the clean URL honors `Accept: text/markdown` with a redirect |
| `/llms.txt` | agents navigating the docs (llmstxt.org shape) | curated URL map of the whole published corpus, plus an in-band "Instructions for LLM agents" block |
| Hosted MCP (`POST /api/mcp/public`) | MCP clients without repo access | six read-only pattern tools, every error carrying a `## Next actions` recovery block |
| Stdio MCP (`mcp/server.ts`) | coding agents with the repo cloned | the same six tools in an ephemeral, network-isolated container |

Repo-level agent instructions live in `AGENTS.md` (the cross-tool convention) and `CLAUDE.md` (Claude Code specifically); both point here rather than duplicating this content.

Live proof: [/showcases/ax](/showcases/ax) exercises every surface with real requests from the browser — the negotiation redirect, `/llms.txt`, a `## Next actions` error, the protocol-version 400, and an interactive `validate_snippet` loop.

## Nothing is hand-maintained

Every artifact derives from an existing single source of truth, because a parallel corpus that needs manual sync is the documented failure mode of this whole genre (Astro removed its llms.txt over exactly that):

| Artifact | Derived from |
|----------|--------------|
| `.md` responses | `getManifest()` / `getRawMarkdown()` (`src/lib/server/docs/manifest.ts`) — the raw glob is consulted only after a manifest hit, so a blocked or draft doc is structurally unreachable (`src/lib/server/docs/markdown-urls.ts`) |
| `/llms.txt` | `buildLlmsTxt(getManifest())` — it cannot drift from the docs, and its test round-trips every emitted URL through the `.md` resolver |
| `validate_snippet` rules | `mcp/snippet-rules.json` (shared by both MCP runtimes) + the `--color-*` names extracted from `src/app.css` at load time |
| README Pattern Index (the marker-delimited region) | `pattern-library/registry.json` via `scripts/patterns/build-derived.ts` (`patterns:build`; staleness gated by `patterns:check`) |
| `docs/pattern-library/*.md` (one page per pattern in its own docs section, → `/docs`, RAG, `/llms.txt`) | the same registry + generator — pointer pages only, never copied prose |
| `/docs/pattern-library` (the section's catalog index: every pattern + purpose) | the same registry, projected live by `#lib/server/patterns/catalog.ts` — no build step |

## The negotiation contract

Cache safety decided the shape, not convenience. HTML at the clean URL is `Vary`-free; the `.md` URL serves its cacheable markdown to agents only and varies on `Sec-Fetch-Dest`; every negotiated redirect is uncacheable:

| Request | Response | Cache-Control | Vary |
|---------|----------|---------------|------|
| `GET /docs/x.md` (agent) | 200 markdown | `public, max-age=0, s-maxage=3600` | `Sec-Fetch-Dest` |
| `GET /docs/x.md` with `sec-fetch-dest: document` (human) | falls through to routing → 303 → `/docs/x` | (redirect, uncached) | — |
| `GET /docs/x` with `Accept: text/markdown` | 303 → `/docs/x.md` | `no-store` | `Accept` |
| `GET /docs/x` (browser) | 200 HTML + `Link: </docs/x.md>; rel="alternate"` | as before | — |

A 308 keyed off a request header without `Vary` would let a shared cache serve the redirect to browsers — that is why the negotiated response is 303 and `no-store`. Wildcards never negotiate (curl's default `Accept` gets HTML), and `sec-fetch-dest: document` never negotiates regardless of the header — a browser navigating to a `.md` URL instead falls through the hook into SvelteKit routing, where the docs layout (`docs/+layout.server.ts`) 303s the suffix away to the rendered page. SvelteKit data requests (`__data.json`, client-router navigations) fall through the same way: serving markdown to them would crash the router's JSON parser. The hook (`docsMarkdown`, stage 4 in `src/hooks.server.ts`) sits above `loadStyle` and `i18n` so no `Set-Cookie` can void `s-maxage` — pinned by an ordering assertion in `handle-chain.gate.test.ts`.

Discovery is layered so an agent finds the map from any entry point: every `/docs` response carries `Link: </llms.txt>; rel="llms-txt"`, doc HTML heads carry `<link rel="alternate" type="text/markdown">`, robots.txt names `/llms.txt`, and `AGENTS.md` lists all four surfaces.

## Self-correcting MCP errors

Every registry-produced tool error ends with a fixed-heading text block:

```
## Next actions
1. `search_patterns` {"query":"pattern"} — lists every pattern in the library.
```

The convention (each rule is a test assertion in `diag.test.ts` / `next-actions.gate.test.ts`):

- the heading is the exact literal `## Next actions` — one grep-able anchor on both surfaces;
- 1–3 numbered entries: backticked tool name, compact JSON args, one clause of *why*;
- argument values are always literals the registry wrote, never caller text — the block adds no echo surface;
- suggested tools exist on the *same* trust surface (a public error never names an admin tool);
- it is **text**, not a structured field — both surfaces are text-only because `structuredContent` makes Claude Code hide the text body entirely.

The hosted `errorResult(body, diag, next)` requires the actions at compile time, mirroring the reasoning that made `diag` required: a new error branch that strands the caller must be a compile error, not a review miss. The transport's two bare literals (unknown-tool, tool-threw) deliberately carry *neither* `diag` *nor* the block — that absence is the telemetry discriminator, and it now signals in both channels.

## validate_snippet

The sixth pattern tool closes the loop `svelte-autofixer` pioneered: submit a snippet, get deterministic line-numbered findings with fixes and doc links, resubmit until clean. It mechanizes the conventions that were previously enforceable only by review: Svelte 5 runes (no `export let`, no `$:`, no stores), component-first, design tokens (including the opacity-modifier trap), Valibot over Zod.

Contracts worth knowing:

- **Findings are a success, not an error.** An `isError` would make agent loops treat the normal case as failure, and it would pollute the `mcp.call_log` capability-gaps meter. Only malformed arguments are errors.
- **Oversize snippets are refused, never truncated** (20 000 chars) — a partially validated snippet reads as clean.
- **The report never echoes snippet content** — findings are `rule at line:column` only, and the argument is named `snippet` precisely because telemetry's `extractQuery` does not read it. Three independent barriers keep caller code out of the call log, pinned by `observer.snippet.test.ts`.
- **The stdio server is a one-directional superset**: it adds a `Bun.Transpiler` syntax pre-check (`syntax-error`) the hosted surface never emits, and it degrades *visibly* (a report footer) if `src/app.css` is unreadable.

## Links and routing stay resolvable

A context file is only as good as the paths it routes to, and practitioner surveys find stale
references in roughly a quarter of AI config files. Two gates keep v10r's from rotting:

- **Instruction files route to paths that exist.** `src/lib/agent-instructions.gate.test.ts`
  reads `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/skills/**`. Every backticked repo path, and
  every bare `name/` in a routing table, must resolve. A path named on purpose as absent ("there is no `src/lib/server/i18n/` yet") is an allowance with a reason, and the
  allowance fails once the sentence or the absence goes away. The same files must carry no
  hidden bidi or zero-width characters, the rule-file backdoor class: instructions an agent
  obeys that a reviewer never sees in the diff.
- **Anchors resolve to headings the page renders.** `patterns:validate` resolves every
  `#fragment` in a registry doc ref through `headingAnchors()`
  (`src/lib/docs/heading-anchors.server.ts`), which runs the docs renderer's own
  `remark → rehype-slug` chain. The README TOC's `anchorFor` goes through the same helper, so one
  slugger serves the gate, the TOC and the rendered page.

Not covered: anchors inside chatbot answers. `catalog-citations.ts` still strips the fragment
before it checks a route. Verifying it at runtime would need a per-page heading index on every
turn, and the cited route already lands on the right page.

## Known limitations and anti-goals

- `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-site` is stamped on every response, so a *browser-context* cross-origin fetch of `/llms.txt` or a `.md` page is blocked. CLI and server-side fetches — the actual agent path — are unaffected. Deliberate: weakening the header for everyone to serve one edge case is the wrong trade.
- **No `llms-full.txt`.** The size-ladder pattern serves frameworks with millions of consumers; here it would be a second corpus to maintain.
- **No SEO motivation.** Google states Search ignores llms.txt; two 100k+-domain studies found zero citation effect. These surfaces exist for agents already fetching v10r, not for crawlers.
- **English only, locale-invariant.** The docs corpus is English by design; `.md` URLs are unprefixed and locale-prefixed variants 308 to them.

# Agentic architecture — decision record

Decisions of the 2026-11-24 initiative. Each names the alternative it beat and what would
reverse it. Decisions about the MCP *server* stay in
[../mcp-evolution/decision-record.md](../mcp-evolution/decision-record.md) (D1–D10); D10 —
*official, maintained protocol implementations by default; custom protocol code needs a
demonstrated necessity* — governs every decision below.

## AA1 — One application architecture, many doors

**Decision.** No standard gets its own registry, orchestrator, permission system or trace.
Every protocol is an adapter that ends in an existing mechanism: tools in `TOOL_MANIFEST`,
runs in the one orchestrator, writes through the approval gate, results through the
untrusted-content boundary, evidence in the turn trace.

**Alternatives.** Adopting an agent framework (Mastra, LangGraph, ADK) as the new runtime
because it already speaks A2A/AG-UI/MCP. Rejected: each brings its own tool registry, memory,
approval and trace model; v10r would run two architectures and translate between them.

**Reverse when** a workload needs an execution model the AI SDK loop cannot express (a
long-lived multi-agent graph with its own persistence) — then the framework enters as an
external A2A peer first, not as the core.

## AA2 — Risk comes from the effect, never from the door

**Decision.** `ToolRisk` (`read` · `view` · `create` · `write` · `destructive`) and `ToolReach`
are assigned by v10r. An MCP `readOnlyHint`, an A2A skill tag, a WebMCP annotation, an A2UI
button or an AG-UI frontend-tool declaration is an *untrusted hint*: it may raise a risk
(`destructiveHint` → `destructive`), never lower one. The MCP spec says the same: "clients
MUST consider tool annotations to be untrusted unless they come from trusted servers."

**Held by** `mcp-client` gate test (no external tool below `write` unless operator-listed),
`webmcp.ts` (only `read`/`view` publishable), the generative-UI action type (view only),
`client-actions.gate.test.ts` (unchanged).

## AA3 — Consume MCP with the official client, not `@ai-sdk/mcp`

**Decision.** `@modelcontextprotocol/client` 2.4.0 — the same major as the server v10r
already runs — inside a framework-free domain. External tools are *projected* into catalogue
vocabulary (`mcp_<peer>_<tool>`, v10r risk, `reach: external`, `resultOrigin: user`).

**Alternatives.** `@ai-sdk/mcp` `createMCPClient`: convenient, converts to AI SDK tools, but
it is the AI SDK's own protocol implementation (no `@modelcontextprotocol/*` dependency) and
its v6 line stops at protocol 2025-11-25 — choosing it would mean a second, non-official MCP
implementation and an AI SDK v7 dependency for this one feature.

**Reverse when** `@ai-sdk/mcp` is built on the official SDK, or after the v7 upgrade if the
conversion helpers remove more code than the projection keeps.

## AA4 — Wired through one external-operations door (revised 2026-11-24, Phase III)

**Was.** The MCP and A2A clients were domains with tests and interop runs, not callable from a
turn, until an admin peer configuration, approval cards and a quota existed.

**Decision now.** Both are wired to the deskbot through `server/external-operations/`: an
operator peer directory (`/admin/ai/peers` for MCP, `A2A_DELEGATION_PEERS` for A2A), a
disclosure the user authorizes per call (separate from mutation risk; reads too), a persistent
atomic claim in `ai.agent_external_operation` with a dispatch marker and lease healing, no
automatic retry, `unknown` kept as `unknown`. The deskbot because it is the authenticated
surface with the persisted proposal door; the chatbot stays read-only. Quota: the delegation
budget (1 per turn, 3 per conversation, depth 1) and the MCP byte caps.

**Reverse when** a surface other than the deskbot needs external calls (then: the same door),
or OAuth peers are wanted (a separate extension).

## AA5 — A2A as an adapter over deterministic architecture checks

**Decision.** v10r serves one A2A agent — the architecture review specialist — whose skills
run `checkSecurity` / `checkArchitecture` (Architecture Studio's engine) over a submitted
model. No model call, no quota, no state beyond the request. The client delegates to
allowlisted peers and types every answer as a **claim** (`status: 'claimed'`), validated and
bounded, never as verified evidence.

**Alternatives.** (a) Expose the chatbot as an A2A agent: every task would spend provider
quota on behalf of anonymous callers and re-open prompt-injection surfaces; rejected for
now. (b) Agents-as-tools inside one runtime: simpler, and still the right choice *inside*
v10r; A2A is for agents another team, language or framework owns. (c) Direct REST between
services: right when both ends are yours and the contract is fixed (`external-service.md`).

**Interop evidence.** An independently implemented Python `a2a-sdk` agent (a performance
specialist with its own rules) is called by v10r's JS client, and a Python client calls v10r's
server — both directions, two languages, two SDKs. The JS server uses `InMemoryTaskStore`
only because no task outlives its request.

**Reverse when** a task must outlive a request (then a database `TaskStore` and durable
execution, AA11) or a caller needs authenticated skills (then a security scheme on the card).

## AA6 — Generative UI: A2UI v1.0, Express for the model, a v10r catalog for the renderer

**Decision.** Three roles, decided separately by measurement (bench report in
[generative-ui.md](../../ai/generative-ui.md)):

| Role | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Model-output language | A2UI **Express**, compiled server-side to v1.0 messages | ~half the tokens of A2UI JSON (131 vs 252 on the reference UI), official compiler, streams |
| Internal renderer | Thin Svelte 5 adapter over the **lit-free root of `@a2ui/web_core`**, a v10r catalog mapped onto `#lib/components`, lazy-loaded | Official processor; component-first and token rules hold; never imports the Lit catalog |
| Interop protocol | **A2UI v1.0** | The only cross-vendor protocol of the three |

The prior research's stop condition ("park it if `web_core` needs a UI framework at run
time") was tested and **not triggered**: the root entry bundles with zero Lit bytes; only
`./universal` and `./catalogs/basic/v1` import Lit, and v10r imports neither (gate test).

**Alternatives.** json-render (official Svelte 5 renderer, ~4 KB gzip core): far lighter, but
no A2UI interop beyond a v0.8 docs recipe — choosing it internally would force custom A2UI
translation code. Kept as the measured fallback. OpenUI Lang: fewest tokens (103) but its
Svelte binding lags two majors and its package runs install-time telemetry — rejected.
Tool-driven cards: remain the baseline and the right choice when the shape is known.

**Reverse when** the lazy chunk becomes a problem on the chat route, or `web_core` breaks its
lit-free root.

## AA7 — Agent Skills are generated, never written

**Decision.** `skills/` is a generated surface of the pattern registry (`skills:build`,
`skills:check` in `validate`), spec-valid per agentskills.io. The registry stays the one
source; docs pages, MCP tools, the RAG corpus and skills are projections of it.

**Alternatives.** Hand-written skills (a second body of knowledge that drifts); serving them
through the MCP skills extension (SEP-2640 is Final, but the SDK support is "being
implemented") — deferred, not rejected.

## AA8 — AG-UI is a projection of the stream we already send

**Decision.** `createAgUiProjector` maps AI SDK UI message chunks to AG-UI events, checked
against `@ag-ui/core`'s own schemas. A client action is AG-UI's frontend tool unchanged.
`POST /api/ai/ag-ui/deskbot` is the adapter: it maps a `RunAgentInput` onto the deskbot's own
request, runs the same orchestrator turn and pipes the projector into SSE under the
deny-by-default policy. The deskbot first, because its loop holds both semantics the
protocol must carry (client actions, the approval boundary). A client cannot fabricate what
it does not own: a server tool result replays only under the ticket the server issued it
with, `state` and `resume` are refused, and decisions go through the approve route.

**Alternatives.** Replacing the AI SDK transport with AG-UI (no Svelte client, no evidence of
benefit); CopilotKit (React-only); a `[surface]` route (the chatbot's boundary work —
page context, surface-action admission — has no AG-UI mapping yet); AG-UI interrupts for
approvals (the approve route already holds the state machine; a resume payload would be a
second door to it).

**Reverse when** a third-party AG-UI frontend needs the chatbot, client-owned state or
interrupt-shaped approvals.

## AA9 — WebMCP publishes client-action contracts, nothing else

**Decision.** `exposeClientActionsToWebMcp` registers existing contracts with
`document.modelContext` when it exists. Same validation, runner, timeouts and bounded
results; only `read`/`view` actions; 30 calls per minute; withdrawn on dispose. Not mounted
on the Desk (the Desk is being refactored) — the Lab page uses it with its own actions.

**Reverse when** Chrome ships WebMCP (157 planned): then the refactored Desk mounts it.

## AA10 — Vercel UI SDK: monitor, do not adopt

Beta (0.1.0-beta.16), overlaps `#lib/components`; its agent layer (snapshot/act/query) is
documented only in secondary sources. Its idea — components that describe themselves to an
agent — is the same as client actions with a read-back. **Reverse at** 1.0 with a documented
AI SDK integration, and only as behaviours under existing components.

## AA11 — Durable execution: no runtime until a run must outlive a request

Every v10r turn finishes inside its request; the approval gate already persists a plan
across requests (proposal → approve → replay with receipts). MCP Tasks and A2A tasks are
protocol handles, not durability. **Adopt the Workflow SDK** (first-party SvelteKit plugin,
hooks for human approval, `WorkflowAgent` on AI SDK v7) **when** a concrete workload needs
minutes-long or restart-surviving runs — accepting the Vercel World lock-in, or Inngest if not.

## AA12 — OpenTelemetry: project the trace, add no tracer

`projectTurnTraceToGenAiSpans` turns a `TurnTrace` into `invoke_agent` / `chat` /
`execute_tool` spans with GenAI attribute names, `v10r.*` for v10r facts, and **no content,
by construction**. The trace remains the audit-grade record; telemetry is a lossy export.
An exporter (`@vercel/otel`, `instrumentation.server.ts`) is an operator choice.

## AA13 — AI SDK v7 is a prerequisite, on its own branch

GA since 2026-06-25 and where `WorkflowAgent`, `toolApproval`, `@ai-sdk/otel` and MCP Apps
helpers live; but `usage` semantics change (multi-step totals) and touch the trace's token
rows, the middleware moves to the V4 provider spec, and Svelte lacks the MCP Apps renderer.
Mixing that into protocol experiments would hide regressions. Planned as wave A′ in
[plan.md](./plan.md).

**Measured (2026-11-24, throwaway worktree, not committed):** bumping to `ai@7.0.170`,
`@ai-sdk/svelte@5.0.170` and the providers at major 4 gives **40 type errors in 5 files** —
11 in `chat-orchestrator.ts` (the tool-execution-end event lost `durationMs` / `success` /
`output` / `error`), 1 in `profile/manifest.ts` (a tool `description` may now be a function),
28 in three test files (`ToolExecutionOptions` gained a context) — and **1 of 766 AI tests
fails**: `model-call-middleware.test.ts`, the trace middleware's stream pass-through. The
trace is exactly where the upgrade bites, which is why it gets its own branch and a recorded
live turn.

**Built (2026-11-24, branch `claude/cloud/ai-sdk-v7`):** `ai` 7.0.179, `@ai-sdk/svelte`
5.0.179, `@ai-sdk/{google,groq,openai}` 4.x (the newest the 24 h install cooldown allows).
All 41 type errors fixed without an `any` or a compat shim; the trace keeps its meaning —
`onStepEnd`'s usage is one model call, the result's `usage` is the sum that is charged, and a
test pins both. Two behavioural changes needed code, not renames: the stateless
`toUIMessageStream` replaces the deprecated result method (with `redactToolErrors: true`
pinned), and an empty model stream now arrives as `NoOutputGeneratedError`, mapped back to the
rotating `EMPTY_ANSWER`. The browser chat client moves from the v5 line (`@ai-sdk/svelte` 3
carried its own `ai@5`) to the server's v7 — one `ai` copy. `toolApproval`, the MCP Apps
helpers, harness skills, `WorkflowAgent` and `@ai-sdk/otel` were read and **not adopted**: none
replaces the proposal → approve → receipt → revert gate, and `@ai-sdk/mcp` 2.x is still its own
protocol code (D10). What cannot be proven without a provider key is one chatbot turn and one
approved deskbot write per provider. Record: [../../ai/ai-sdk-v7.md](../../ai/ai-sdk-v7.md).

## AA14 — Deferred and rejected, with triggers

| Technology | Decision | Trigger to revisit |
|---|---|---|
| MCP Apps provider | Experiment (built on a branch: pattern explorer, [mcp-apps.md](../../ai/mcp-apps.md)) | A recorded external-host run; the compat kit run with a `_meta.ui` case |
| MCP Apps host | Defer | A sandbox origin and a concrete third-party app |
| ACP | Defer (future pattern) | Remote transport leaves RFD; Studio "hand to a coding agent" is scheduled |
| AGNTCY, ANP, registries | Monitor | A partner requires DID/VC identity or a registry reaches GA |

# Agentic security — one trust model across every door

Every interop door (MCP server and client, A2A server and client, AG-UI, WebMCP, generative
surfaces, Agent Skills) is held to the rules the in-app assistant already follows. This page
lists them once.

## Operation classes

An operation is classified by what it does; the class decides the gate. The door it arrives
through decides nothing.

| Class | Example | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| Presentation | Render a generative surface, stream text | None — data, not code; catalog allowlist |
| Local interaction | Type into a surface field, toggle a checkbox | None — local data model, no round trip |
| Read | Search patterns, list files, review an architecture model | Auth/ownership as the caller; bounded results |
| View change | Open or focus a panel (client action, WebMCP) | `view` risk: auto, budgeted, read back |
| Persistent creation | Create a desk file | `create`: auto with notification (unchanged) |
| Persistent modification | Edit a file | `write`: proposal → human approval → replay with receipts |
| Destructive | Delete | `destructive`: explicit confirm |
| External communication | Call an external MCP tool | `reach: external` → approval-gated (untrusted-content gate) |
| Remote delegation | Send a task to an A2A peer | Operator-listed peer and skill; `reach: external` → disclosed, human-approved external operation, once; budget one per turn, depth one; result is a *claim* |
| Remote execution | Run code a model produced | **Never** — rejected in every form |

## Requested, executed, confirmed — and claimed

v10r already separates *requested* (the call left), *executed* (a handler ran) and *confirmed*
(the state was observed afterwards). Remote agents add a fourth word: **claimed** — a peer
says it did something. A2A artifacts, MCP tool results and WebMCP callers' reports are
claims: validated against a schema, bounded, wrapped as untrusted content, never used as an
authorization input and never shown as verified. An A2A delegation receipt keeps the five
apart: approved (requested), sent (executed, with `delivery`), `succeeded` (the peer
*claims* a completed review), a cancel the peer confirmed (still its claim), and never
*verified*.

## Threats and where each is held

| Threat | Held by |
|---|---|
| Prompt injection via external content | `resultOrigin: 'user'` → `<untrusted-content>` for every external result (MCP client, A2A client) |
| Forged tool results in the history a client sends | Chat and desk turns: every server tool result in the request is replaced by the copy the conversation's rows hold; one the rows do not hold reaches the model wrapped as untrusted content whatever the tool's declared origin (`ai/recorded-tool-results.ts`); client action results go through their own contract door (`client-action-results.ts`); the AG-UI endpoint admits a replayed server result only under its ticket. None of these results ever authorized anything: approvals are proposal rows |
| Tool poisoning (lying descriptions/annotations) | Annotations never lower risk (AA2); descriptions prefixed as external; drift fingerprint forces re-approval |
| Malformed interface definitions | A2UI catalog validation (unknown components/props, depth, size, binding paths, URL schemes) before render; renderer never uses `{@html}` |
| Unauthorized state change | Only server tools change data, only after approval; surface actions, WebMCP and AG-UI frontend tools are view-risk. The AG-UI endpoint takes only declared client actions from `RunAgentInput.tools`, admits a replayed server tool result only under the ticket it issued (`ai/ag-ui/tool-result-ticket.ts`), and refuses `state` and `resume`, so a client cannot fabricate a tool result or an approval |
| Cross-tenant leakage | Domain functions are owner-scoped; A2A server skill is stateless and holds no user data |
| Credential exposure / token passthrough | MCP and A2A clients never forward a session or user token: the shared peer egress drops `cookie`, `authorization` and `proxy-authorization` and sends only the peer's own bearer, by secret reference (`MCP_PEER_SECRET_*`, `A2A_PEER_SECRET_*`) |
| Delegated permissions | A peer gets nothing v10r did not decide to send; no OAuth delegation is built |
| Data exfiltration through tool arguments | The content screen before every proposal: secrets (deployment values, credential shapes) and relayed `<untrusted-content>` refused; arguments that quote what the turn read (`quotes_read_content`) run only with a separate quoted-content authorization on the card; the complete outgoing arguments shown on the card under the approval's argument digest (64 KiB bound); the operator's field allowlist and byte cap; every external call, read or write, approval-gated. The screen is defense-in-depth, not DLP: a paraphrase is not caught |
| Unreviewed peers or tools | Peers and tools exist only in the operator's directory (`/admin/ai/peers`); a tool runs only at the fingerprint the operator activated; revocation and drift are re-checked at verify and before the send |
| Replay / duplicate execution | Client-action runner dedups by call id; WebMCP calls are budgeted (no shared call id); proposals replay once; an approved MCP peer call or A2A delegation runs once per approval: in the product the claim is a row in `ai.agent_external_operation` (one transaction with the proposal, one winner across instances, a dispatch marker before the send, a stale claim healed to `failed`/`not_sent` or `unknown`/`possibly_sent`, never re-run), and an unknown outcome is never retried ([external-operations.md](../../ai/external-operations.md)); an A2A delegation binds the agent card digest, the operator policy and the arguments digest, so a changed card, policy or model refuses; a surface action naming a superseded render is `stale_surface` |
| SSRF | Peer allowlist; https only; private, link-local, loopback and metadata addresses refused; redirects are errors. MCP and A2A clients share one secured transport (`http/peer-egress.ts`): DNS answered once, every address checked, the socket pinned to the checked address with SNI, certificate check and `Host` kept for the name (`http/pinned-fetch.ts`), so a rebinding answer cannot redirect the call; private destinations only as an exact range plus port (`PrivateDestination`), link-local never. The pinned connect bypasses `HTTPS_PROXY`: a proxy-only deployment cannot reach peers ([agent-to-agent.md](../../ai/agent-to-agent.md#secured-transport-shared-with-the-mcp-client)) |
| Sandbox escape | No third-party HTML is hosted (MCP Apps host deferred) |
| Resource exhaustion | Body caps, result caps, tool-count caps, per-turn and per-minute budgets, timeouts with abort; A2A: 512 KiB per response, 64 stream events, one delegation per turn and three per conversation, `CancelTask` after a timeout or abort |
| Excessive token consumption | Express format; catalog pruning; bounded tool lists from peers |
| Recursive delegation | v10r's A2A skills run deterministic checks, no assistant, so an inbound task cannot reach `delegate_architecture_review`; the delegation budget refuses any proposal from a turn at depth ≥ 1 and more than one per turn; outgoing messages carry `v10r.delegationDepth: 1` |

## What is not claimed

No penetration test was run. The adversarial suites are unit and in-process interop tests
with hostile fixtures; the Python peers are local processes, not hostile networks.
