| Airtable field model | Field ids (`fld…`), 32 field types, select options carry `id` + `name` [V] | Established | n/a | n/a | Proprietary | Model to emulate (option ids) |
| Baserow | Real Postgres table per table, real column `field_{id}` per field [V] | Established | Runtime DDL | n/a (Vue/Django) | MIT core + premium [V] | Contrast: shared-schema tables, not inline |

| Keystatic / TinaCMS | Code-defined schema, git/markdown-backed [U] | Established-ish | n/a | n/a | MIT [U] | Not runtime-editable; low relevance |

| Automerge 2 | CRDT, Rust/WASM core [U] | Established | n/a | Framework-agnostic | MIT [U] | Not justified for MVP |

### 2. Data-model prior art

#### Notion [V]
- Property object: `{ id, name, description, type, <type>: {config} }`. "A property's `id` stays the same
  when its name changes." The title property always has id `title`. Ids are URL-encoded in responses.
- Types include checkbox, date, email, files, formula, multi_select, number, people, phone_number,
  relation, rich_text, rollup, select, status, title, unique_id, url; computed types (formula, rollup,
  created/edited) are read-only.
- Select options: names unique case-insensitively, no commas.
- Since API version `2025-09-03`, schemas belong to *data sources*, not databases: evidence that even
  Notion moved its schema boundary once. Keep the definition/instance boundary explicit.
- Notion's schema is **shared per database** (not inline per page). v10r's inline design is closer to a
  free-form "property bag"; the id/name/type/config shape still transfers directly.

#### Airtable [V]
- 32 field types; field ids look like `fldXXXXXXXXXXXXXX`; formulas store ids, UI shows names.
- Select **options have their own ids**; writing an unknown option name fails unless `typecast`.
  Lesson: give select options stable ids, or a rename of an option silently orphans stored values.
- Multi-select update replaces the whole array (no element-level patch).

#### Baserow [V] / Directus [V] / NocoDB [U]
- Baserow: a real Postgres table per user table, a real column `field_{id}` per field. Columns are
  named by **id**, never by label (same lesson as Notion).
- Directus: "fields are database columns with additional metadata"; "alias" fields have no column.
- These are **runtime-DDL** systems: they `ALTER TABLE` on user action. That fits shared schemas across
  many rows, but it costs migrations, locks and a privileged DB role. It is the wrong fit for inline,
  per-record attributes.
- Licensing: Baserow core MIT; Directus v12 "Monospace Sustainable Core License", source-available and
  GPLv3 after 4 years (previously BSL with a $5M grant) [V]. Neither is something to embed; both are
  only architecture references.

#### Contentful [V]
- Two-step field deletion: mark the field "omitted" (reversible: it disappears from responses), then
  delete permanently. A cheap, valuable UX/safety pattern for "remove attribute".

#### Payload CMS [V]
- Rich field vocabulary (Array, Blocks, Group, JSON, Relationship, Select, Upload…) defined in TS
  config; "presentational" and "virtual" fields are separated from data fields. Useful taxonomy:
  v10r's attribute kinds are *data* kinds; layout/grouping is a separate concern.

### 3. Form generators

#### Form.io [V]
- Definitions embed **JavaScript strings** (custom conditionals, calculated values, custom validation).
  Form.io itself ships a "Protected Evaluator" (`@formio/protected-eval`, based on JS-Interpreter) so
  that owners can sandbox "unsafe, user-supplied code". The existence of that plugin is the warning.
- CVE-2020-28246 (`formio`): server-side template injection leading to RCE; NVD 9.8; the vendor disputes
  it (sandboxed, admin-only); Snyk lists no fixed version and says the default template service was
  removed after 2020.
- Verdict: never accept code-as-data. If v10r ever needs conditions, use a closed, declarative
  operator set (e.g. `{ when: attrId, equals: value }`) evaluated by a tiny interpreter.

#### JSON Forms [V]
- JSON Schema (data) + UI Schema (layout) separation; renderer sets for React (Material, Vanilla),
  Angular (Material) and Vue 3 (Vanilla, Vuetify). **No Svelte renderer set.** Validation via Ajv.

#### SurveyJS [V]
- Only the *Form Library* (the renderer) is MIT. The *Survey Creator* (the builder UI, which is the
  part matching "user adds attributes") requires a paid developer license per team member.

#### react-jsonschema-form [V]
- Very active (v6.11.1 on 2026-11-05) but React-only.

#### svelte-jsonschema-form (`@sjsf/form`) [V]
- Svelte 5 native; MIT AND Apache-2.0 (contains modified rjsf code). Validators: Ajv8, cfworker,
  schemasafe, **Valibot**, Zod4. Current line 3.3.x [S, ecosyste.ms]; ~170 GitHub stars: one maintainer,
  small community (bus-factor risk).
- It *renders* a schema; the v10r pattern's core is *editing the schema itself* inline with values.
  Adopting it would add a JSON Schema layer, a theme package and a validator adapter just to render
  eight simple kinds, while v10r already has its own component library (component-first rule).

### 4. Validators: JSON Schema vs Valibot

- **Ajv** [V]: compiles schemas with code generation. In browsers it needs CSP `'unsafe-eval'`
  ("not recommended", enables XSS) unless schemas are **precompiled at build time** (standalone code).
  User-authored schemas are by definition runtime, so precompiling is impossible. Ajv's own docs say
  schemas must be "trusted as your application code": untrusted ones can cause stack overflow and slow
  compilation, and `pattern`/`patternProperties` risk ReDoS. Mitigations: `code: { regExp: RE2 }`
  (changes regex semantics, no look-aheads), `maxLength`, no `allErrors` in production.
- **@cfworker/json-schema** [V]: interpreting validator (exists because Workers lack the APIs Ajv
  compilation needs), supports 2020-12, 113 kB unpacked. The safe choice *if* JSON Schema is required at
  runtime.
- **`@valibot/to-json-schema`** [V]: Valibot to JSON Schema **draft-07**; `errorMode`
  `'throw' | 'warn' | 'ignore'`; transformations "have no equivalent in JSON schema". Recent additions:
  `typeMode` (input/output), `overrideSchema/Action/Ref`, `addGlobalDefs`, `toJsonSchemaDefs`. No
  documented `fromJsonSchema` [V: not mentioned]. Good for *exporting* the attribute document shape (for
  MCP tools, AI tool schemas, OpenAPI), not as a runtime engine for user schemas.
- **Key design point**: the user-authored "schema" here is a closed vocabulary of 8 kinds plus a few
  options (required, min/max, options, maxLength). That is not arbitrary JSON Schema. A fixed Valibot
  *variant over `kind`* validates both the definition and the value with no code generation, no
  user regex, and server/client parity. Build-time Valibot schemas are trusted application code.

### 5. Storage: JSONB vs EAV in PostgreSQL

#### JSONB semantics [V, PostgreSQL docs]
- `jsonb` "does not preserve white space, does not preserve the order of object keys, and does not keep
  duplicate object keys. If duplicate keys are specified in the input, only the last value is kept."
  Short keys are stored before longer ones.
  - Consequence 1: **attribute order cannot live in object key order.** Store attributes as an
    **array** (order = array index), or carry an explicit `position`.
  - Consequence 2: a duplicate-key payload is silently collapsed on the server (last wins), while the
    client may have used the first one. Validate uniqueness of attribute ids *before* insert. Never rely on
    `jsonb` to reject duplicates.
- `jsonb` rejects numbers outside `numeric` range, `\u0000`, and NaN/Infinity. Validate numbers as finite
  and strip NUL in the domain, or the insert fails late with a DB error.
- Docs: "any update acquires a row-level lock on the whole row. Consider limiting JSON documents to a
  manageable size."
- Size: no numeric jsonb limit in the datatype page [V]; ~255 MB per jsonb value is a commonly cited
  implementation limit (JEntry offset bits) [S]; general field limit 1 GB [U]. Irrelevant at our scale;
  set an application cap (e.g. ≤ 200 attributes, ≤ 64 kB document).

#### Indexing [V]
- GIN `jsonb_ops` (default): supports `?`, `?|`, `?&`, `@>`, `@?`, `@@`; one index entry per key *and*
  value.
- GIN `jsonb_path_ops`: supports `@>`, `@?`, `@@` only (no key-exists), entries per value; "usually much
  smaller… specificity of searches is better"; no entries for empty structures such as `{"a": {}}`.
- With an **array of attributes** (`[{id,label,kind,value}]`), containment queries like
  `attributes @> '[{"label":"Color","value":"red"}]'` work with `jsonb_path_ops`. Hot, known attributes are
  better served by an **expression index** or a generated column (btree) on a specific path.

#### TOAST and rewrites [S, pganalyze 2022]
- Values larger than ~2 kB get compressed or moved out of line (TOAST); reads of TOASTed jsonb are
  markedly slower; **any update duplicates the whole TOASTed value** (WAL + bloat). Partial-update patches
  for TOAST were proposed (PG15 era), not merged as of that source.
- MVCC: every UPDATE writes a new row version anyway [U, standard PG behavior]. Small documents (well under
  2 kB, typical for a handful of attributes) avoid the TOAST cliff entirely.

#### EAV
- EAV (`record_id, attribute_id, value_text/value_num/...`) gives per-attribute rows, typed columns and
  FK references. Costs: N-way self-joins or pivots to rebuild a record, loss of per-type constraints
  unless one column per type exists, many rows per record, harder atomic "save whole record"
  [U, well-known trade-offs].
- Systems that need shared schemas at scale (Baserow, Directus) chose neither: they chose **real columns
  via runtime DDL**. EAV appears mostly in legacy commerce platforms (e.g. Magento) [U].
- For *inline, per-record, small* attribute sets that load and save as one unit, **JSONB is the
  established fit.** Use EAV or relational columns only for attributes that must be referentially
  enforced or heavily queried across records; promote those to real columns.
- "reference" kind: a JSONB value cannot carry a FK. Either validate existence in the domain on write
  and tolerate dangling refs on read, or mirror refs into a side table (`record_reference`) with real
  FKs [design option, not a library fact].

### 6. Binary formats (CBOR, MessagePack)

- CBOR is RFC 8949 (2020) [U text]; §4.2 defines "deterministic encoding" (preferred/shortest
  serialization, definite lengths, map keys sorted bytewise by encoded form) [U, search hits on dCBOR /
  CBOR-core drafts confirm active follow-up work]. MessagePack has a stable spec, no deterministic profile
  [U].
- cbor-x's own benchmark (author-run, unspecified dataset) [S]: JSON encode 16.4k ops/s vs cbor-x 32.3k;
  decode JSON 17.7k vs cbor-x 18.9k (75k with "shared structures"); @msgpack/msgpack decode 14.2k (slower
  than JSON.parse). The gains come mainly from record/shared-structure extensions, not plain CBOR.
- For small documents (≤ a few kB) over HTTP with gzip/brotli: size differences shrink to near zero
  after compression, V8 `JSON.parse` is highly optimized, and **Postgres stores jsonb, not CBOR**, so a
  binary wire format adds an encode/decode hop at each end plus a dependency. DevTools, logs and
  SvelteKit form actions are JSON-native. **No measurable benefit for the MVP** (claim based on the
  above, not a v10r-specific benchmark).
- If byte-stable hashing is ever needed (signatures, dedup), **RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization Scheme**
  [U] keeps JSON and gives determinism without a binary format.

### 7. Schema evolution

- **Stable ids vs labels** (Notion [V], Airtable [V], Baserow `field_{id}` [V]): every production system
  keys by an immutable id and treats the label as mutable display text. Renames are then free, and
  values survive. Select options need ids too (Airtable [V]).
- **Cambria** (Ink & Switch, 2020) [V]: bidirectional lenses (rename, convert, wrap, head, add, remove,
  in, hoist) over JSON Patch, translate-on-read through a graph of schemas. Explicitly a **research
  prototype**, not production-quality; limitations: lossy changes, no recursion, no cross-document,
  unmeasured performance. Experimental; take the *idea*, not the library.
- **Versioned documents + upcasters** (event-sourcing practice) [U, established practice]: store
  `schemaVersion` in the document; on read, run pure `v1→v2→v3` functions in the domain; write back at
  the latest version. Simple, testable, no dependency. Fits "no backward compatibility" during
  development (a one-off rewrite script is equally valid), while keeping the pattern honest for
  adopters.
- **Kind change** of an attribute (text→number) is a lossy convert: either forbid it or require an
  explicit, validated conversion with a "value cleared" warning (Cambria's `convert` caveat applies).

### 8. Concurrency and patches

- **Optimistic concurrency** [U text of RFC 9110, established]: a `version` integer (or ETag) per record;
  the client sends `If-Match` (or the version in the form body); the server does
  `UPDATE … WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2` and on 0 rows returns **412 Precondition Failed** (REST) or a
  `fail(409, …)`-style conflict in a form action. Cheapest correct answer for single-author or
  low-contention editing.
- **JSON Patch, RFC 6902** [U]: ordered ops (`add`, `remove`, `replace`, `move`, `copy`, `test`) with JSON
  Pointer paths; `test` gives per-path preconditions; array index paths are fragile under concurrent
  reorders. Using attribute ids (not indices) requires id-to-index resolution.
- **JSON Merge Patch, RFC 7386** [U]: object-merge semantics, `null` means delete (cannot set a value to
  `null`), arrays replaced wholesale. With attributes as an array, merge patch degenerates to
  "replace all": fine for whole-document save.
- **CRDTs**: Yjs ~27.5 kB gzip [S]; Automerge 2 is a Rust/WASM core (larger, async init) [U]. Worth it
  only for real-time multi-user co-editing or offline-first sync; they need a sync server/provider and a
  binary document format (stored as `bytea`, not queryable jsonb). **Not justified for the MVP**;
  whole-document save + version check + clear conflict UX covers the stated use case.

### 9. Security checklist (parsing and user input)

- **Prototype pollution** [V, fastify/secure-json-parse]: `JSON.parse` creates `__proto__` as an *own*
  property ("by itself… not a security issue"); the danger arises on `Object.assign` / spread / deep-merge
  / iteration-copy, where it becomes the prototype. `secure-json-parse` offers `protoAction` /
  `constructorAction` (`error` | `remove` | `ignore`).
  - v10r mitigation without a dependency: attributes are an **array of objects with fixed keys** validated
    by a strict Valibot `object` (unknown keys rejected or stripped), user text lives only in *values*
    and *labels*, never in object *keys*. Reject attribute ids/keys equal to `__proto__`, `constructor`,
    `prototype` via an id regex like `^[a-z0-9_-]{1,32}$` or generated ids. If a lookup map is needed,
    use `Map` or `Object.create(null)`.
- **ReDoS** [V, Ajv security doc]: do **not** offer user-supplied regex patterns in the MVP. If required
  later: length-cap the pattern, compile with a linear-time engine (RE2 / `re2js`) [U for re2js], or offer
  predefined formats (email, url) instead. Cap `maxLength` on all strings regardless.
- **No code in data** (Form.io lesson [V]): no expressions, templates or formulas evaluated from stored
  definitions.
- **Size caps**: attribute count, label length, value length, list length, total document bytes. Bounds
  also protect the TOAST threshold and the row lock duration [V, PG docs].
- **XSS**: render labels/values as text (Svelte escapes by default); never `{@html}` for multiline values.
- **CSP**: avoid any validator needing `unsafe-eval` (Ajv runtime compile) [V].

### 10. Lessons for v10r

1. **Build on Valibot; adopt no form/schema library.** The attribute vocabulary is closed (8 kinds); one
   Valibot variant over `kind` validates definitions and values on server and client, with no codegen,
   no CSP issue and no new dependency. Export with `@valibot/to-json-schema` (draft-07) where an external
   contract needs JSON Schema (MCP/AI tools). Re-evaluate `@sjsf/form` only if a future pattern renders
   *arbitrary external* JSON Schemas.
2. **Shape: Notion's property object, stored inline.** `{ id, label, kind, config, value }` in an
   **ordered array** under a versioned envelope `{ schemaVersion, attributes: [...] }`. Immutable
   generated `id`; mutable `label`; select options with their own ids.
3. **JSONB, not EAV**, for inline, per-record, load-and-save-as-a-unit attributes. Default GIN
   `jsonb_path_ops` only when cross-record containment search is a real requirement; promote hot
   attributes to expression indexes or real columns. Keep documents small (cap) to stay under TOAST.
4. **Order lives in the array**, never in object keys (jsonb reorders keys and drops duplicates,
   last-wins [V]).
5. **Validate before Postgres**: unique ids, finite numbers, no `\u0000`, length caps, strict objects
   (prototype-pollution-safe keys).
6. **Optimistic concurrency** via a `version` column: 412 for the REST surface, a form `fail` for the page
   surface. Whole-document replace on save (Merge-Patch-equivalent); JSON Patch only if granular sync is
   needed later.
7. **Evolution**: `schemaVersion` + pure upcasters in the domain; Cambria as inspiration only
   (research-grade).
8. **Removal UX**: Contentful-style two-step (hide/"omitted", then delete) or undo; kind changes are
   explicit lossy conversions.
9. **Not for MVP**: CBOR/MessagePack (no measurable benefit for small, gzip'd, jsonb-stored documents),
   CRDTs (only for real-time co-editing or offline-first), user regex, any expression language.
10. **Reference kind**: domain-validated id + optional side table with real FKs if integrity matters;
    jsonb cannot enforce FKs.

### Where the implementation departed from these lessons

- The envelope field is `format`, not `schemaVersion`: in v10r *version* is the stored
  record's optimistic-concurrency counter and *revision* a stored pre-image, so the shape
  number needed its own word.
- Seven core kinds, not eight: `reference` was left for later (it needs a domain to validate
  against), and the registry is open, so an application adds its own kinds.
- Removal is a bounded in-record trash (`removed`, restorable in place) plus undo, rather than
  Contentful's two-step omit-then-delete.
- A type change never clears a value: what does not convert exactly is kept in `previous`.
- Conflicts can be merged, not only detected: a three-way merge by attribute id, offered as a
  button, because attribute ids make most concurrent edits disjoint.
- The REST surface answers a stale save with `409 version_conflict` (the desk's existing
  contract), not `412`.

files.docs/blueprint/forms.md: # Forms Architecture Type-safe forms with real-time validation using Superforms and Valibot. > Schema definition, `superValidate`, `superForm`, the Valibot API, and the Valibot-vs-Zod rationale live in the **`valibot-superforms`** skill. This doc covers only v10r's decisions: the hybrid Better-Auth-vs-Superforms split, file locations, project gotchas, and the accessibility patterns this project mandates. --- ## Strategy **Hybrid Approach:** Superforms + Valibot for most forms, Better Auth client for authentication. | Component | Choice | Why | |-----------|--------|-----| | Form library | Superforms v2 | SvelteKit-native, progressive enhancement | | Validation | Valibot | Smaller than Zod, tree-shakeable, fast | | Enhancement | `use:enhance` | No full-page reloads | | Feedback | Inline + Toast | Context-dependent error display | ### Hybrid Approach: When to Use What | Form Type | Use | Why | |-----------|-----|-----| | Email entry (login) | **Better Auth client** | Built-in rate limiting, magic link + OTP | | OTP verification | **Better Auth client** | Token validation, expiry handling | | OAuth flows | **Better Auth client** | Redirect handling built-in | | Profile updates | **Superforms + Valibot** | Not auth-critical, benefits from real-time validation | | Settings / preferences | **Superforms + Valibot** | Standard CRUD, good UX with debounced validation | | Contact / feedback forms | **Superforms + Valibot** | Server actions, email integration | | CRUD operations | **Superforms + Valibot** | Data mutations with optimistic UI | **Rationale:** Better Auth's client methods (`signIn.magicLink`, `signIn.otp`) handle security concerns that Superforms would need to replicate. Using Superforms for auth would mean re-implementing rate limiting, manual CSRF handling, and potential security gaps. See [auth.md](./auth.md#authentication-flows) for Better Auth form implementations. --- ## Schema Location Strategy Schema definition is skill territory; **where** schemas live in v10r is not: | Schema Type | Location | Example | |-------------|----------|---------| | Route-specific | Top of `+page.server.ts` | Login form | | Shared/reused | `#lib/schemas/*.ts` | User profile | | Complex nested | `#lib/schemas/*.ts` | Address, wizard steps | Export `v.InferInput` types alongside each schema for reuse. --- ## Server + Client Wiring The standard loop: `superValidate(valibot(schema))` in `load`, `superValidate(request, valibot(schema))` in the action (return `fail(400, { form })` when invalid), and `superForm(data.form, { validators: valibotClient(schema) })` on the client. The skill covers the generic shape — below are the v10r conventions layered on top. ### Validation Timing **Default: `'auto'` (recommended)** — the research-backed "reward early, validate late" pattern. Validates on **blur** for pristine fields, and on **input** only after errors appear. Don't specify `validationMethod` unless you need to override it. | Question | Answer | Use | |----------|--------|-----| | Need real-time feedback? (password strength, live char count) | Yes | `'oninput'` | | Does validation require a server call? (username availability) | Yes | `'oninput'` + `delayMs: 500` | | Is the form complex with expensive validation? | Yes | `'onblur'` | | Standard form fields? | Yes | `'auto'` (default) | ### Debounce Timing Guidelines Research shows **100-300ms** feels instant; **>300ms** feels sluggish. | Validation Type | Recommended Delay | Rationale | |-----------------|-------------------|-----------| | Client-side only | **150ms** | Fast feedback, no API cost | | Mixed client/server | **300ms** | Balance responsiveness and efficiency | | Async server checks | **500ms** | Reduce API calls, wait for typing pause | --- ## Error Display Patterns Three surfaces: inline field errors, a form-level `$message`, and toast notifications. ### When to Use Each | Context | Error Display | |---------|---------------| | Field validation | Inline under field | | Auth errors (invalid code, expired link) | Form-level message | | Server errors (500) | Toast notification | | Success feedback | Toast notification | | Multi-step wizard | Summary at step top | ### Error Priority Hierarchy When multiple error types occur simultaneously, follow this priority to avoid overwhelming users: | Priority | Error Type | Display Method | Suppress Others? | |----------|------------|----------------|------------------| | 1 (Highest) | Network failure | Toast (error) | Yes — hide form errors | | 2 | Server error (500) | Form-level message | Yes — skip field errors | | 3 | Rate limit exceeded | Form-level message | Yes — skip field errors | | 4 | Auth failure | Form-level message | No | | 5 | Multiple field errors | Inline + focus first | No toast | | 6 (Lowest) | Single field error | Inline only | No | **Implementation** — branch in `onError`/`onResult`, focusing the first invalid field on multi-error failures: ```typescript const { form, errors, enhance, message } = superForm(data.form, { validators: valibotClient(schema), onError({ result }) { // Priority 1: network/connection errors — suppress field errors if (result.error?.message?.includes('fetch')) { toast.error('Connection lost. Please check your network.'); return; } // Priority 2-3: server errors flow through form-level $message }, onResult({ result }) { if (result.type === 'failure') { // Priority 5: focus first invalid field const firstError = document.querySelector('[aria-invalid="true"]'); if (firstError instanceof HTMLElement) firstError.focus(); } if (result.type === 'success') { toast.success('Changes saved!'); } }, }); ``` --- ## Data Invalidation After Form Actions Form actions using `use:enhance` call `refreshAll()` after a successful submission, re-running all load functions on the current page (`page.state` survives). SvelteKit's own `enhance` callback opts out with `update({ refreshAll: false })`; Superforms 3 keeps its option name, `invalidateAll`. Outside a form, call `refreshAll()` from `$app/navigation`; it replaces Kit's `invalidateAll()`. | Pattern | Use Case | Example | |---------|----------|---------| | Superforms `invalidateAll: true` (default) | User login/logout | Update global user state | | `invalidate('/api/items')` | Item CRUD on list page | Refresh items list only | | Superforms `invalidateAll: false` + local state | Real-time preview | Update component state without refetch | | `goto()` + automatic invalidation | Create → Detail page | Navigate + fresh data | | Redirect from server | Create → List page | `redirect(303, '/items')` | ### Optimistic Updates Pattern Set `invalidateAll: false`, mutate local `$state` in `onSubmit`, reconcile with the server item in `onResult`, and roll back in `onError`: ```typescript let items = $state(data.items); const { form, enhance } = superForm(data.form, { invalidateAll: false, onSubmit() { const tempId = `temp_${Date.now()}`; items = [...items, { id: tempId, ...formData }]; }, onResult({ result }) { if (result.type === 'success' && result.data?.item) { items = items.map(i => i.id.startsWith('temp_') ? result.data.item : i); } }, onError() { items = items.filter(i => !i.id.startsWith('temp_')); toast.error('Failed to create item'); }, }); ``` **Prefer a server-side `redirect(303, ...)`** when navigating after a mutation (automatic invalidation). Use client-side `invalidate()` when staying on the page. --- ## Form Patterns ### Edit Form (Loading Existing Data) Pass existing data as the **first** parameter to `superValidate()` to pre-populate the form: ```typescript // load const form = await superValidate(existingUser, valibot(userSchema)); ``` Gate the save button on `$tainted` so it stays disabled until a field actually changes from its pre-populated value: ```typescript const { form, tainted } = superForm(data.form, { validators: valibotClient(userSchema) }); ``` ```svelte ``` ### Reset After Submit Set `resetForm: true` to clear the form back to its initial values after a successful response — the right default for feedback forms, surveys, or anything the user might submit again: ```typescript const { form, enhance, message } = superForm(data.form, { validators: valibotClient(schema), resetForm: true, }); ``` A success message set via `message()` still persists through the reset, so a confirmation can stay visible after the fields clear. ### Multi-Step Wizard Validate the current step before advancing. Compose per-step schemas, then merge for the final submit via `entries` spread: ```typescript export const wizardSchema = v.object({ ...step1Schema.entries, ...step2Schema.entries, ...step3Schema.entries, }); ``` ```typescript const { validate } = superForm(data.form, { validators: valibotClient(schemas[currentStep - 1]), }); async function nextStep() { const result = await validate(); if (result.valid) currentStep++; } ``` ### Dependent Fields (Cascade) Derive child options from the parent value and reset children when the parent changes: ```svelte ``` ### Confirmation Modal Cancel auto-submit in `onSubmit`, show the dialog, then call `submit()` programmatically on confirm: ```typescript const { enhance, submit } = superForm(data.form, { onSubmit({ cancel }) { cancel(); showConfirm = true; }, }); ``` Use the project [`ConfirmDialog`](./design/components.md) composite — not a raw modal. ### Server-Only Validation Errors For conditions only the server can check — a duplicate email, an expired invite code — use `setError()` for a per-field error and `message()` for a form-level one, both from the action: ```typescript import { message, setError, superValidate } from 'sveltekit-superforms'; if (await emailTaken(form.data.email)) { return setError(form, 'email', 'This email is already registered.'); } if (codeExpired) { return message(form, 'This invite code has expired.', { status: 400 }); } ``` These run alongside — not instead of — the synchronous Valibot schema: the schema catches shape errors before submit; `setError`/`message` catch what needs a database lookup. ### File Upload The real file-upload form in v10r is the **image-metadata showcase**: schema in `#lib/schemas/showcase/image-metadata.ts`, server resolver in `#lib/server/imagemeta/`. The upload is processed server-side with Sharp and stored in [R2](../stack/data/r2.md). It validates the **metadata** about the image (title, alt text, keywords, category, optional GPS) through Superforms + Valibot — not the file bytes. The codebase does **not** use Valibot file validators (`v.file`, `v.mimeType`, `v.maxSize`) or `withFiles()` anywhere; file constraints are enforced in the server resolver. > If you do need schema-level file validation in a new form, Valibot v1 offers `v.file` / `v.mimeType` / `v.maxSize`, and Superforms offers `withFiles()` on `fail`. Neither is currently used in this repo. A form that posts files needs `enctype="multipart/form-data"`; client-side preview via `URL.createObjectURL(file)`. ### Array / Dynamic Fields — v10r Gotcha > **Progressive Enhancement Warning:** `dataType: 'json'` **breaks** the no-JS path. The form will NOT work without JavaScript, `use:enhance` is mandatory, and `disabled` is ignored (all `$form` data posts regardless). Only use it for nested objects/arrays where a no-JS fallback isn't required. A top-level array of primitives works in the default `dataType: 'form'` mode **only if each element is backed by a real DOM input named after the field** — Superforms reads it server-side via `formData.getAll('fieldName')`. A `bind:value`-only component that renders no named inputs (a tag-chips / `TagInput`-style component) silently posts an **empty array**: the server receives `[]` and the data is lost. Two fixes: - **Mirror each element in a hidden named input** (progressive-enhancement-friendly — array still posts with JS off): ```svelte {#each $form.keywords as keyword} {/each} ``` - **Switch to `dataType: 'json'`** — but this breaks the no-JS path (see the warning above). ### Async Validation (Server-Side Checks) For username availability / email uniqueness, v10r **does not** use a Valibot async schema. The Superforms schema stays synchronous; the availability check is a separate debounced `fetch` to a dedicated, rate-limited API endpoint, decoupled from Superforms/Valibot validation. The `/showcases/forms/validation/async` example wires it this way: 1. The form validates against a plain sync `v.object` (`asyncSchema` in `#lib/schemas/showcase/validation.ts`) via `superValidate(request, valibot(asyncSchema))`. 2. An `oninput` handler debounces (~400ms), then `fetch`es `/api/showcases/check-username?u=…`, which returns `{ available }`. 3. The endpoint (`src/routes/api/showcases/check-username/+server.ts`) is a rate-limited `GET` — the gate lives server-side, not in the form schema. ```typescript // client — debounced check, independent of Superforms debounceTimer = setTimeout(async () => { const res = await fetch(`/api/showcases/check-username?u=${encodeURIComponent(username)}`); const { data: { available } } = await res.json(); if ($form.username === username) usernameAvailable = available; }, 400); ``` > Valibot does ship async schemas (`v.objectAsync` + `v.pipeAsync` + `v.checkAsync`) for inline server checks, but **v10r does not use them** — the dedicated-endpoint pattern above is the project convention. --- ## Draft recovery **Problem.** A long form is lost to a closed tab, a crash, a dead battery or an expired session, and the usual defence — a "Leave site?" prompt on every dirty form — guards none of those and trains people to click through it. The opposite mistake is just as common: a draft restored on its own, so a stale value is submitted without anyone noticing, or a draft written to a shared browser where the next account reads it. **Method.** Keep what was typed, offer it back, guard only what could not be kept. | Piece | Where | Rule | |---|---|---| | Draft store | `src/lib/state/form-draft.ts` | `localStorage` key `v10r:form-draft::`, envelope `{ v, savedAt, data }`. A read keeps only the form's own fields with the form's types; a write drops credential-like names (password, token, card, …) and `exclude`d fields. Storage is injected and every failure is "no draft" | | Superforms binding | `src/lib/state/form-draft.svelte.ts` | `createFormDraft(sf, { formId, owner })`: debounced writes while tainted, a stored draft that differs from the form becomes an **offer**, `clear()` in `onUpdated` on a valid submit. Storage is touched only in `$effect`, so SSR and hydration agree | | Offer UI | `DraftRecoveryNotice` (composite) | Restore or discard. A draft is never applied without a click | | Leave guard | `src/lib/state/leave-guard.svelte.ts` | `guardUnsavedChanges(isDirty, message)`: one `beforeNavigate` — a `confirm` for in-app navigation, `cancel()` for `type === 'leave'` so the browser shows its own unload prompt. No own `beforeunload` listener | **Guard only what is lost.** A form whose draft was written loses nothing on leave, so its guard predicate is `isTainted() && draft.saveFailed` — the prompt appears only when the browser refused the write (quota, private mode). A component with no draft (the palette workshop) guards plain `dirty`. **Sign-out erases drafts on purpose.** Sign-out sends `Clear-Site-Data: "storage"`; a draft is a convenience for the person at this browser, not a record, and it must not outlive their session on a shared machine. Work that has to survive sign-out is a server-side draft (`versioned-document-session`), not this. **Invariants.** - A draft is offered, never applied on its own, and never offered when it equals the form. - No credential-like field and no field outside the form's shape is ever written. - Drafts are keyed per account; another account in the same browser sees none. - A valid submit clears the draft. Live: `/showcases/forms/advanced/draft`. ## Mobile UX ### Input Types and inputmode Use the right combination of `type`, `inputmode`, and `autocomplete`: | Field Type | type | inputmode | autocomplete | |------------|------|-----------|--------------| | Email | `email` | `email` | `email` | | Phone | `tel` | `tel` | `tel` | | Numeric code | `text` | `numeric` | `one-time-code` | | Decimal price | `text` | `decimal` | — | | URL | `url` | `url` | `url` | | Search | `search` | `search` | — | 2FA code field: `type="text" inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="one-time-code" pattern="[0-9]*" maxlength="6"`. ### Touch Targets | Standard | Level | Minimum Size | |----------|-------|--------------| | WCAG 2.2 | AA (required) | 24×24 CSS px | | WCAG 2.1 | AAA (recommended) | 44×44 CSS px | ### iOS Safari Zoom Prevention iOS Safari zooms in on inputs with `font-size < 16px`. Use the accessible fix: ```css input, select, textarea { font-size: max(16px, 1rem); } ``` **Never use** `maximum-scale=1` in the viewport meta tag — it breaks accessibility by preventing all user zooming. --- ## Accessibility These patterns are **mandated** for v10r forms. | Requirement | Implementation | |-------------|----------------| | **Labels** | Every input has an associated `

# Derivation

Most stored data in an application is derived: chunks and embeddings from documents, generated
pages from a registry, a wasm binary from a crate. Every derived output carries the same three
questions. Is it still current? Can it be rebuilt and checked? Where did it come from? Each
section below answers one of them.

## Derivation key

**Problem.** A content hash tells you the input bytes have not changed. It cannot tell you
that the code reading them has. When the chunker changes, every document hash stays
identical and every stored chunk goes stale. v10r's docs ingest used to skip on content hash
alone, so a chunking change needed someone to remember `--force`. When nobody did, the
assistant answered from chunks the current code would never produce.

**Method.** Store a key beside every derived output:

```ts
derivationKey(transform, inputs)   // src/lib/server/db/content-hash.ts
// = contentHash(JSON.stringify([transform, ...inputs]))
```

- `transform` names the producing code and its version: `docs-ingest@1`,
  `retrieval-ingest@1`. Bump it when that code changes what it writes.
- `inputs` lists everything else that changes the output, in a fixed order: the source's
  content hash, the chunker's `chunkingInput()` (logic version plus sizing), the embedding
  model, and the context model that wrote the prefixes (or `no-context-model`).
- The output is current exactly while a recomputed key equals the stored one. A null key
  (derived before keys existed) never matches, so such an output re-derives once.

**Where it runs.**

| Derivation | Transform | Reader that skips on a match |
|---|---|---|
| Docs corpus (`scripts/db/ingest-docs.ts`) | `docs-ingest@N` | Per file. An unchanged corpus costs zero embeds, and a run cut short by the embed quota resumes where it stopped |
| Desk files (`retrieval/ingest/index.ts` → `ingestIfChanged`) | `retrieval-ingest@N` | `syncDeskFileToRetrieval`, offered every pinned file by the daily `desk-retrieval-sync`. Unchanged inputs keep their embeddings and the copy is re-stamped current; a chunker or model bump re-derives every copy. Only a `ready` copy's key counts, because an errored ingest stored its key too |

**Keeping the version honest.** A version constant is only as good as the discipline of
bumping it. So `plan.test.ts` pins a fingerprint of the chunker's *output* on a fixture next
to `CHUNKER_VERSION`. If the planner's behaviour changes, the test fails, and whoever changed
it has to decide: bump the version (and re-derive every corpus) or show the change is
output-neutral. Hashing the chunker's source code instead was rejected. A comment edit would
re-embed the whole corpus and use up the day's embedding quota.

**Graphs, briefly.** Selective recomputation across a dependency graph uses the same key
applied per node: a node is dirty when its key moves, and its dependents re-key on the new
output. v10r has two small graphs and needs no general engine. The spreadsheet resolver
(`src/lib/desk/formula.ts`) memoises per pass and reports cycles as `#CIRC!`. `topoSort` in
`pattern-library/schema.ts` orders the registry's `depends_on` deterministically, and
`patterns:validate` fails on a cycle.

**Invariants.**

- Every input that changes the output is either listed in `inputs` or covered by the
  transform version. An undeclared input is the one way the key lies.
- The key is written in the same insert as the output it describes.
- A missing key means stale, never fresh.
- Exactly one place builds each shared input (`chunkingInput()`, `EMBEDDING_INPUT`), so two
  producers of the same derivation cannot key it differently.
- Only a successfully derived output's key counts. A failed derivation that stored its key
  must not satisfy the next comparison.

**Do not use** when a full rebuild is cheap and nothing reads a stale output in between, as
with the pattern pages, which are regenerated from scratch on every build. A key there would
only add bookkeeping.

## Reproducible artifact build

**Problem.** Some outputs are committed to the repository: generated docs, a snapshot of
MCP excerpts, a wasm binary. A committed artifact has to stay provably in step with its
sources. "Run the generator before you commit" is prose, and prose drifts.

**Method.** The proof depends on whether the gate can run the generator:

| Case | Proof | v10r instance |
|---|---|---|
| The generator runs in the gate (deterministic, cheap, no network) | **Regenerate and diff.** `--check` rebuilds in memory and fails on any byte difference, any missing output, or any orphan | `patterns:check` (README index plus one page per record, with orphan pages detected), `mcp:excerpts:check` (single snapshot file, byte-compared) |
| The generator cannot run in the gate (a Rust toolchain in a pinned container) | **Manifest plus digest recheck.** The build writes the sha256 of every input and output plus the toolchain identity; the gate recomputes the digests | `scripts/wasm/build.sh` → `src/lib/wasm/kernel/build-manifest.json` (image pinned by `@sha256`, `wasm-bindgen` version, inputs, outputs) checked by `kernel-manifest.test.ts` |
| The output depends on the build environment (bundle size) | **Attested snapshot.** The record carries what is needed to reproduce it, and the gate refuses one without it | `perf/snapshot.json` must carry `gitSha` and `NODE_ENV=production` (`snapshot.gate.test.ts`) |

The manifest follows the shape of SLSA provenance (`buildType`, resolved dependencies with
digests, subjects with digests), unsigned. Signing and SLSA build levels only matter when a
third party verifies the artifact. Wall-clock time stays out of manifests, so the manifest is
itself reproducible.

**Bit-for-bit vs input-addressed.** The pattern pages are bit-for-bit reproducible: the same
registry always gives the same bytes. The wasm manifest proves something weaker. The files
present now match the files hashed at build time. It does not prove that a rebuild would
produce the same binary. `kernel-manifest.test.ts` says so in its own header. Outputs of
non-deterministic transforms, such as embeddings and LLM context prefixes, are
**input-addressed**: their derivation key proves which inputs produced them, never that a
rerun would match. Label each artifact with the kind of proof it actually has.

**Invariants.**

- A committed artifact is checked by the gate. A generator with no check is an unbound mirror.
- `--check` fails on missing and orphaned outputs, not only on changed bytes.
- Generators read neither the clock nor the network, and iterate in a declared order.
- A manifest's toolchain identity is pinned by digest, not by tag.

**Do not use** for outputs that are never committed and are rebuilt on every deploy (the
SvelteKit build itself), where the deploy *is* the regeneration.

## Provenance record

**Problem.** "Where did this come from?" covers several questions. Which input was it derived
from? Which activity produced it? Was that a person or a model, and on whose behalf? Without
a common shape, every feature invents its own half-answer, and the halves do not line up.

**Method.** Use the core of W3C PROV-DM and nothing more: an **entity** (the thing, pinned to
a revision or content hash, never to a mutable id alone), an **activity** (what produced it,
with its transform version), and an **agent** (`human`, `software` or `ai`, plus on whose
behalf). Three relations carry it: *generated by*, *derived from*, and *attributed to*.
OpenLineage is pipeline-level and full PROV-O/RDF exists for exchange between organisations;
both are overkill for an application.

| v10r instance | Entity pinned by | Activity / transform | Agent |
|---|---|---|---|
| `blog.revision` + `blog.published_revision` | immutable revision row + `contentHash` | publish | author user id |
| `retrieval.document` / `chunk` | `contentHash` + `derivationKey` | `docs-ingest@N` / `retrieval-ingest@N` | system or owning user |
| `image_metadata.fieldProvenance` | per field | AI proposal vs human edit | `ai-draft` / `human`, plus `approvedBy` |
| `desk.file_revision` | pre-image row | the overwrite that replaced it | `source: ai \| user` |
| `TurnTrace` (`ai.turn`, `model_call`) | `profileVersion`, provider + model ids | one assistant turn | the model, on behalf of the user |
| `admin.audit_log` | before/after in `detail` | privileged action | admin user id |
| `build-manifest.json` | input and output sha256 | `build.sh` with a pinned image | the build |

`provenance` is also the name of `TurnProvenance` (`authored` / `recorded` / `live`). That is
one instance of the same concept: where a shown turn came from. It is not a second meaning.

**Invariants.**

- Provenance points at a revision or a content hash, never only at a mutable id. Otherwise it
  dangles after the next edit.
- AI and human authorship are distinguished at the field or row where they differ.
- Agent references are personal data, so each trail decides explicitly what happens on
  account erasure, and the schema states the decision. v10r uses all three answers:
  `desk.file_revision` cascades with its user, `blog.revision.author_id` is set to null (the
  revision outlives its author), and `admin.audit_log.actor_id` deliberately has no foreign
  key, so the record of a privileged action survives the account that took it.
- Provenance is append-only. A correction is a new record, not an edit of the old one.

**Do not use** for data with one author and no derivation, such as a user's own settings row,
where the row is its own provenance.

# Execution

Work that outlives one request, or one tab, has to leave the world in a known state when
something dies halfway through. The two patterns here cover the two places that happens. On
the server, a run is interrupted between steps. In the browser, a document session is
interrupted between saves.

## Durable step execution

**Problem.** A multi-step operation (deliver a notification, replay an approved plan, reset a
database branch) can be killed by a timeout, a deploy or a crash. A retry then has to answer
three questions. What already happened? Who owns the work now? Can the old worker still write?

**Method.** v10r has three hand-rolled implementations of the same contract. It does not use
a workflow engine; `docs/stack/vendors.md` records why Inngest and Trigger.dev were passed
over. Here is the contract they share:

| Element | What it guarantees | Outbox (`notifications/outbox.ts`) | Approved plan (`db/ai/proposals.ts` + `ai/proposals/execute-proposal.ts`) | Branch reset (`dbops/operations.ts`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Status machine** | Every transition is a conditional `UPDATE … WHERE status = <from>`, so exactly one caller wins | `pending → processing → sent \| failed \| dead` (a retry is `pending` again with `attempts > 0`) | `pending → approved → executing → executed \| failed` (+ `expired`, `rejected`) | `queued → running → succeeded \| failed \| canceled` |
| **Claim** | Exactly one worker owns the run | `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` claim that bumps `attempts` | `markExecuting`'s conditional `approved → executing` | one-in-flight guard + `idempotency_key` under a unique index |
| **Lease + reaper** | A dead owner is detected, never waited on forever | 5-minute claim lease, `reclaimStaleDeliveries` | 120 s per-step heartbeat, `markInterruptedIfStale` heals lazily on the next read | lease checked on every poll, `dbops-reaper` job |
| **Fence** | A stale owner cannot write after losing the lease | terminal writes match `attempts = <claimed>` | `lockExecuting` locks the row in each step's transaction and refuses unless still `executing` | every transition guarded on `status = 'running'` |
| **Receipts** | What committed is recorded *with* the effect, not after it | the delivery row itself | `agent_proposal_step`, PK `(proposal_id, step_index)`, written in the step's own transaction | `neonOpStatuses` on the row |
| **Retry policy** | Retries are bounded and spaced | exponential backoff on `next_attempt_at`, `dead` after max attempts | none: a failed step is a receipt, and a new plan is a new proposal | none: the external operation is polled, never re-issued |

**Lease time is the database clock.** The outbox and the proposals compare and stamp leases
with Postgres `now()`, the same clock their claim predicates read. A serverless instance's
`Date.now()` is a second, skewable opinion. `dbops` still computes its lease in application
time. That is acceptable there because the lease is generous and only guards crashes, but it
is a deviation, recorded as one.

**Exactly-once is a claim about the record, not the world.** The receipt and the database
mutation commit together, so a database effect happens exactly once per step. An external
side effect such as an email, a Telegram message or a Neon API call happens *at least once*.
A worker whose lease lapsed mid-send can send again after a reclaim. The outbox accepts
this, because a duplicate notification is cheaper than a lost one. `dbops` avoids it by never
re-issuing the external call: it only polls the operation it started.

**Compensation is not atomicity.** An approved plan stops at the first step that is not
`ok`, and the steps before it stay committed. Undoing them is a separate, compensating run
with its own receipts. No cross-step rollback is ever claimed.

**Invariants.**

- Every transition is conditional on the state it leaves; a transition that matches no row
  is a lost race, not an error.
- A lease is always paired with a fence. Without one, a stalled owner commits behind a
  terminal status.
- A step's receipt commits in the same transaction as the step's database effect.
- Step identity is stable across retries: a position in a frozen payload, or a row id. It is
  never a counter of calls made so far.
- A terminal run answers every repeat request from its receipts and never re-executes.
- External effects are at-least-once unless the external API takes an idempotency key, and
  each implementation says which it is.

**Do not use** for a single-statement mutation, where one transaction is already all-or-
nothing. And do not grow this into a workflow engine. Long sleeps, fan-out and hundreds of
steps are where a durable-execution platform (Vercel Workflow, Temporal) earns its cost. Know
its limits before adopting it: Vercel Workflow keeps run state in its own store, not your
database, and replay-based engines break on code changes to in-flight runs.

## Versioned document session

**Problem.** A user edits a document in the browser while the server, another tab or an AI
write can change the same document. Saves fail on flaky networks. The tab can close mid-save.
The aim is that no edit is ever lost silently and no overwrite is ever silent either.

**Method.** The server stays authoritative and every save carries the version it was based
on. The client is a small state machine around that, owned by the document rather than by a
component. In v10r it is generic over the document's content — `#lib/state/document-autosave.ts`
and `document-drafts.ts` — and each document kind wires it: `spreadsheet-session.svelte.ts`
for sheets, `record-session.svelte.ts` for [dynamic-attribute records](../dynamic-attributes/pattern.md).

- **Save queue.** Edits debounce into one latest snapshot, and requests are serialised. An
  edit made while a save is in flight stays pending; a success never clears it.
- **Compare-and-swap.** `PUT /api/desk/files/[id]` requires `expectedVersion`. A mismatch is
  `409 version_conflict`, and the session enters an explicit `conflict` state. There is no
  automatic rebase. A document kind that can merge offers it as a button: `rebase(resolve)`
  hands the kind's merge the confirmed base, the local copy and the stored one, and saves the
  result against the stored version (records merge by attribute id; sheets do not merge).
- **Per-writer drafts.** Every unsaved snapshot is written to its own localStorage slot
  (`v10r:spreadsheet-draft:{user}:{file}:{writerId}`), so one tab never erases another's
  draft. On load, sibling drafts are offered to adopt or discard, never applied silently.
- **Stale-read guard.** Out-of-order reads, and reads that raced a local edit, are dropped
  using a read sequence and a generation counter.
- **Reload that cannot destroy work.** `discardAndReload()` fetches first and replaces
  local state only once the fetch succeeded, so going offline does not erase the only copy.

**Why not a CRDT.** Sync engines converge on server-authoritative writes even when their
reads are local-first: Zero moved permissions into server mutators, and Electric and PowerSync
send writes through your API. A CRDT pays for itself in concurrent rich-text co-editing. It
costs bundle size (about 232 KB gzipped for Zero's client), an unsolved authorisation story,
and merge semantics that cells with formulas do not have. An explicit conflict on a
spreadsheet cell is more honest than a silent merge.

**Invariants.**

- Every save carries its base version, and the server rejects a stale one.
- Unsaved work exists in exactly one place per writer, and nothing deletes it until a save
  of that work succeeded or the user discarded it.
- A conflict is a state the user resolves; it is never resolved by last-write-wins.
- The session's lifetime is the document's, not a component's. Closing a panel flushes,
  never drops.

**Do not use** for append-only input such as a chat message or a form submission, where a
plain request with an idempotency key suffices. Or for data no one else writes, where the
version check never fires. Reach for a CRDT only when two people must type into the same
paragraph at the same time.

# Truth

Two questions a reader of any fact needs answered: **who owns it**, and **how sure are we**.
The principle behind the first is in
[foundation/self-expressive-project.md](../../foundation/self-expressive-project.md); this
file is the method for making it executable.

## Source-of-truth gate

**Problem.** A fact recorded twice will eventually disagree with itself. The second copy is
usually there for a good reason: a client bundle cannot import the server schema, a public
page must show the policy a job enforces, a script runs without the app's bundler. "Keep them
in sync" is prose, and prose drifts.

**Method.** Every fact gets exactly one owner. Every other place that needs the fact holds
one of these, listed from cheapest to most expensive:

| Binding | How the copy stays true | v10r instance |
|---|---|---|
| **Typed** | The compiler refuses a missing or extra key | `retention-copy.ts` is typed `Record<RetentionRuleId, …>`, so a rule with no reader-facing copy does not compile |
| **Imported** | The copy *is* the owner, reached by import | `doc-filter.ts` is imported by both the `/docs` routes and `scripts/db/ingest-docs.ts`; `content-hash.ts` is the one hash used by blog, retrieval and `content:check`; `pattern-library/query.ts` is the one implementation of the registry tools behind both MCP transports (`mcp/patterns/parity.test.ts` executes both and diffs the answers) |
| **Generated + `--check`** | The copy is rebuilt from the owner and the gate diffs the bytes | README Pattern Index and `docs/pattern-library/` (`patterns:check`), `mcp/public-excerpts.snapshot.json` (`mcp:excerpts:check`) |
| **Drift test** | The copy is hand-held, and a test compares it to the owner | `db-enums.drift.test.ts` (client enum mirror vs `pgEnum`, member order included), `schema-filter.gate.test.ts` (`drizzle.config.ts` vs declared `pgSchema`s), `credits/registry.gate.test.ts` (credited SPDX id vs the installed package) |

Two rules make a drift test trustworthy:

- **A non-empty control.** A gate that iterates over a list passes vacuously when the list is
  empty. `credits/registry.gate.test.ts` asserts each scan found entries, and
  `naming.gate.test.ts` asserts it scanned more than a thousand files.
- **Allowances that only shrink.** An exemption list is an argument for keeping something,
  not a place to hide it. `naming.gate` and `architecture.gate` fail on a *stale* allowance
  as well as on a new violation, so the list cannot outlive its reason.

**Fail closed when the owner cannot be read.** Precedence between two sources is resolved at
design time by choosing one owner, never at runtime by falling back. `loadProviderRegistry`
(`src/lib/server/ai/index.ts`) is the reference: the database is the only source of AI
provider configuration. An unreadable table is an error, and a key that will not decrypt
marks the registry `degraded`. Neither falls back to environment variables, and neither
reads as "nothing configured". A fallback to a second source is exactly the second source of
truth this pattern exists to remove.

**Invariants.**

- One fact, one owner. A second writable copy is a defect, not a configuration choice.
- Every non-owner copy is typed, imported, generated or drift-tested, and no other kind exists.
- A drift test proves its own scan was non-empty.
- Exemption lists fail when an entry no longer applies.
- Reading the owner either succeeds or fails loudly; it never silently substitutes another
  source.

**Do not use** for a value read in one place only: the owner and the reader are the same
line, and a gate around it is ceremony. And do not build a runtime "authority service" to
arbitrate between sources. If two candidates need arbitrating, there is one owner too many.

## Evidence status dimensions

**Problem.** "How sure are we?" is several questions, and collapsing them into one score
makes every one of them unanswerable. A 0.8 does not say whether the model was confident,
whether a human checked, whether all sources responded, or whether the answer is a year old.

**Method.** Keep each dimension in its own field, named for what it measures:

| Dimension | Question | v10r instance |
|---|---|---|
| **Verdict / signal** | What does the evidence suggest? Named so it never claims more than that | `NameConflictSignal` (`level` + `reasons`), deliberately not `risk score`, `verdict` or `safe` (`src/lib/name-check/report.ts`) |
| **Coverage** | How far did we look, and what could not be checked? | `NameCoverageStatus` per source: `complete`, `unavailable`, `quota_exhausted`, `credentials_missing`, `timed_out`, `manual_only` |
| **Method and confidence** | Who or what produced it, and how confident was the producer? | `ai_proposal.confidence` (the model's own tier per field), kept apart from `fieldProvenance` (`empty` / `ai-draft` / `human`), the record of who wrote the value (`src/lib/schemas/image-metadata.ts`) |
| **Use** | How far did a source get into an output? | `TurnItemState`: `available` → `considered` → `included` → `executed` → `cited`. Inclusion never claims influence (`src/lib/types/turn-trace.ts`) |
| **Grounding** | Does the claimed reference still resolve? | `CatalogCitationStatus`: `exists` / `drifted` / `none` (`src/lib/server/ai/catalog-citations.ts`) |
| **Proof grade** | What machine-checkable evidence backs it? | `PatternMaturity`: `proven` holds only with a linked test or showcase plus `verifiedAt` (`pattern-library/schema.ts`) |
| **Freshness** | When was it checked, and when does it go stale? | `retrievedAt` on name-check matches, `verifiedAt` plus the 180-day staleness warning in `patterns:validate` |
| **Aspiration vs floor** | Is this where we want to be, or a line we must not cross? | Perf targets (reported, never fail a build) vs ratchets (fail the gate) in `src/lib/server/perf/budgets.ts` |

**Invariants.**

- Distinct dimensions get distinct fields. A single score that merges confidence, coverage,
  provenance and freshness is never stored.
- A grade is only as fine as a machine can verify. Rungs that rest on self-declaration rot,
  which is why `PatternMaturity` has three values and not six.
- Field and type names describe the evidence, not a conclusion (`signal`, `coverage`,
  `drifted`, not `safe`, `verified`, `valid`).
- Self-reported confidence never stands in for acceptance. A model's `high` and a human's
  approval are separate facts.
- Missing coverage is a value, not an absence. An unanswered source is recorded as such,
  never left out of the count.

**Do not use** for internal values nobody reads as evidence (a cache hit flag needs no
confidence model), or where one boolean is honestly the whole story.

## Asset rights manifest

**Problem.** An app that ships third-party models, photos or fonts owes their authors the
attribution their licenses require. In v10r that obligation lived in two hand-kept
`ATTRIBUTION.md` files beside the assets, while the code that displays the assets carried a
second, partly different credit string. No gate tied the two together, and two CC BY 4.0 models
were shown in the app with no attribution at all.

**Method.** The module that owns an asset owns its rights record, beside the data that uses it:

```ts
interface AssetRights { author: string; license: string /* SPDX id */; source: string /* https */ }
```

- `#lib/3d/models.ts` (`Model3D.rights`) and `#lib/3d/parts.ts` (`PartPhoto.rights`) are the
  owners. `#lib/credits/asset-rights.ts` holds the type and the reading helpers
  (`requiresAttribution`, `licenseLabel`, `creditLine`).
- `#lib/credits/registry.ts` *derives* `assetCredits` from the owners. Nothing is re-typed.
- Every surface that shows an asset renders `creditLine(rights)`: the part-photo lightbox, and
  `/credits` for everything.
- `credits/registry.gate.test.ts` lists every file under `static/models/` and
  `static/images/parts/` and fails unless each is credited exactly once. It also checks every
  license is a well-formed SPDX id (`LicenseRef-PublicDomain` where a source dedicates no
  license) and every attribution-requiring license carries an author and an https source.
- The license identifiers come from the [SPDX License List](https://spdx.org/licenses/). For
  repository files outside the app, [REUSE](https://reuse.software/spec-3.3/) sidecars are the
  equivalent convention.

**What the gate does not prove.** That a license *permits* the use. Compatibility depends on how
an asset is used (modified, redistributed, commercial), which an identifier does not encode, and
automated compatibility checkers answer "uncertain" for exactly the interesting cases. The gate
checks that the metadata is present, well-formed and rendered. Whether the use is allowed stays
a human, and sometimes legal, judgement.

**Invariants.**

- Every shipped third-party file has exactly one rights record, owned by the module that uses it.
- No second attribution copy exists beside the files. The record is derived into every surface.
- A license that requires attribution is rendered wherever the asset is credited.
- Rights metadata is never presented as a legal conclusion.

**Do not use** for first-party assets the project made itself, or for npm dependencies, whose
license metadata the package already carries (the credits registry checks those against
`node_modules` instead).

# Name check — search aggregation over unreliable registries

A public, no-login pre-screen for a proposed brand, product or project name: what already
exists that could conflict with it. One report from several upstreams of uneven
reliability — trade mark registries, company registers, RDAP, web search — with per-source
coverage, dependency-free name similarity, and a descriptive conflict signal that never
claims legal availability.

**Page:** `/showcases/name-check` · **API:** `POST /api/name-check` · **Domain:**
`src/lib/server/name-check/` · **Contract:** `src/lib/name-check/report.ts` ·
**Schema:** `src/lib/schemas/name-check.ts`

## The problem it solves

Clearing a name means searching six databases by hand and reconciling what they say. Each
one has a different API story: EUIPO has an official one behind a registered app, GLEIF is
keyless, DPMA sells a contract, WIPO and USPTO publish none, domain registries speak RDAP
(some of them), and "is anyone already trading under this name" is a web search. The
feature treats that as a **search aggregation problem**: one query, every source at once,
partial results as a first-class outcome.

What it deliberately is not: a trademark clearance. The report says what was found and
where the search could not look. It never says "available", "safe", or a risk percentage —
`report.ts` has no field that could render as one.

## Vocabulary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **name check** | The feature. Domain `name-check/`, route `/showcases/name-check`, API `/api/name-check`, keys `showcase_name_check_*`. |
| `NameSource` | One upstream: `id`, `kind`, `territories`, `manualUrl()`, optional `configured()` and `search()`. No `search` ⇒ manual-only. Not "adapter" (`*.adapter.ts` is the transport seam) and not bare "source" (turn provenance). |
| `NameMatch` | One finding, discriminated on `kind`: `trademark` · `company` · `domain` · `web`. Each kind has its own facts; every one carries `similarity`, `jurisdiction`, `territoryRelevance`, `url`, `retrievedAt`. |
| `NameSimilarity` | `{ score 0–100, basis }`. Shown as "name similarity", never as a probability of anything. |
| `NameCheckCoverage` | Per source: `complete` · `unavailable` · `quota_exhausted` · `credentials_missing` · `timed_out` · `manual_only`, plus the manual URL, `retrievedAt`, `cached`. |
| `NameConflictSignal` | `level` (`none` · `similar` · `potential` · `strong`) + `reasons` (codes with params, localised on the page) + `manualReviewRecommended`. |
| `territory` vs `jurisdiction` | The query's scope (`de` · `eu` · `worldwide`) vs a record's origin (`DE`, `EM` for an EU mark, `WO` for an international registration). |

## Pipeline

```
+page.server.ts actions.check ─┐
                               ├─► checkName(query, deps)
POST /api/name-check ──────────┘        │  per source: territory filter → configured? →
                                        │  readThrough(cache) → breaker → daily quota →
                                        │  bulkhead → deadline.child(6 s) → source.search()
                                        ▼
        normalize → sources (concurrent) → dedupe → similarity → relevance → signal → report
```

- **Normalisation** (`normalize.ts`): NFKD, accents and `ß` folded, lowercase, punctuation
  and hyphens dropped, a leading article and trailing legal forms stripped.
  "The Velo-Raptor!" and "veloraptor" are the same key. One normaliser for every name the
  check touches — the query and every candidate.
- **Similarity** (`similarity.ts`): exact → normalised → edit distance (≤ 2) → Kölner
  Phonetik → shared dominant token → affix containment → bigram floor. The best rung wins
  and names itself as `basis`, which is what the page shows beside the score. Bands mirror
  the spec: 100 / 100 / 94 / 88 / 81 / ~62. Nothing below `SIMILARITY_FLOOR` (60) is shown.
- **Relevance**: `nice-classes.ts` maps a category to Nice classes and grades a mark
  `same` · `possibly` · `unrelated` · `unknown` — unrelated is still shown, never dismissed.
  `relevance.ts` grades a jurisdiction against the territory; an EU mark is `same` for
  Germany, an international registration `overlapping`.
- **Signal** (`signal.ts`): explicit predicates. *Strong* = near-exact, live, same
  territory, same category. *Potential* = close mark in a related category, or near-exact
  with the category unknown, or an active exact company in the territory, or a registered
  exact domain plus web usage. *Similar* = anything above the floor. `manualReviewRecommended`
  is set at `potential` and above, and whenever a trade mark source in scope was not
  searched — for a German territory that is always, because DPMA cannot be.

## Sources

| Source | Kind | Access | What a miss means |
|---|---|---|---|
| EUIPO (`sources/euipo.ts`) | trademark | Official API; OAuth2 client credentials + `X-IBM-Client-Id`, saved as a source connection. Hosts are part of the connection because the Sandbox portal runs on its own `api-sandbox` / `auth-sandbox` hosts; the production hosts are the defaults. The Sandbox answers from EUIPO's *sample* register (a frozen snapshot with synthetic rows, not aligned with production) — right for the admin connection test, wrong for real answers. Production access is free: identity documents (passport/ID, or ID plus a company-register excerpt) e-mailed to `docs.apiplatform@euipo.europa.eu`; the Conditions of Use permit showing results publicly. Two RSQL queries: contained term (quoted when the name has spaces) and prefix. | No EU trade mark or EU-designating international mark matched. |
| GLEIF (`sources/gleif.ts`) | company | Keyless JSON:API; full-text + fuzzy completions; 60 req/min. | No **LEI holder** by that name. Most companies have no LEI — this is a signal, not a register. |
| RDAP (`sources/rdap.ts`) | domain | IANA bootstrap (cached 24 h, static fallback); public servers the bootstrap omits by override — DENIC's pilot for `.de`, Identity Digital for `.io`, SWITCH for `.ch`; DNS delegation as evidence for `.eu` (no RDAP); `lookup_unavailable` for the rest. 200 → registered, 404 → not registered, else unknown. | The domain is not registered at that registry. Says nothing about a mark. |
| Web (`sources/web.ts`) | web | Vendor seam: the first connected of Tavily then Brave, else `credentials_missing`. Exact-phrase query — Tavily additionally with `exact_match`, so pages merely *about* similar names do not count, and a German boost (`country`) for the German territory — ten hits, graded on host label and title. | Nothing on the web's first page used the name. |
| DPMA, TMview, WIPO, USPTO, Handelsregister, OpenCorporates (`sources/manual.ts`) | trademark / company | Manual links only: no API, a paid contract, or terms that forbid scripted access. | Not searched. The coverage row says so. |

Every source declares `manualUrl()` and the coverage table shows it on every row — the
authoritative search is one click away whether the automated one ran or not.

## Resilience and spend

A source that cannot answer becomes a coverage row, never an error response
(`check.ts`, `coverageStatusFor`). Around each live source, in this order:

- `readThrough` on a shared cache policy — 24 h for registries, 1 h for domains — keyed by
  `<source>:<sha256(searchInputs)>`. Each `LiveNameSource` declares in `searchInputs` what
  its `search` reads that can change the answer — EUIPO its RSQL queries and API base (the
  sandbox/production switch), the web source its vendor, the exact typed phrase and Tavily's
  country, GLEIF the canonical name, RDAP the compact label — never a secret. Keying by the
  compact name alone served "Velo Raptor" the web hits for "VeloRaptor". Only successes are
  cached; a cached failure would replay an outage for a day. The envelope keeps the upstream
  `retrievedAt`.
- One `defineBreaker` for the domain, subject = source id: three failures in two minutes
  opens it for five; a 429 trips it for `Retry-After`.
- `takeDailyQuota` (`quota.ts`): per-source counters in Redis, sized to the free tiers in
  `config.ts` (`DAILY_QUOTA`). Fails open — the counter protects a bill, not a boundary.
- `defineBulkhead` per source (8 slots for RDAP's ten lookups, 4 elsewhere).
- `deadline.child(SOURCE_CEILING_MS)` inside the request's own budget: the fan-out takes
  8 s of the 10 s hook budget and holds 700 ms back for the response.

The per-IP limiter (`RATE_LIMIT_*`, 10 per minute) runs **before** any of this, on both the
form action and the JSON route, with the honeypot in front of it on the form.

## Privacy

The name a visitor types may be an unreleased brand. Therefore: POST bodies, never `?q=`;
no log line carries the name (errors are logged by class and status, `fetch-json.ts` never
logs a URL or body); the cache key is a hash; no table stores a query; the report is
returned and forgotten. The privacy showcase and `docs/stack/vendors.md` list the upstreams
the name is sent to.

## What the UI never says

- "Legally available", "safe to use", or any percentage that could read as legal risk.
- A similarity score without its basis.
- "No matches" without the coverage table beside it saying *where* — the closing note on
  the page spells out that it means "in the sources marked complete".
- A colour without a word: every level and status pairs its Badge or Alert with text.

## Source connections

Vendor credentials are **administrator-managed and persisted**, never environment-based —
the same shape as the AI providers' `ai.provider_connection`
(`docs/blueprint/ai/provider-routing.md`). The admin connects each vendor under
**Admin → Name check** (`/admin/name-check`): enable it, enter EUIPO's client id and secret
or a search API key, test, save. `.env` carries nothing for this feature; `ENCRYPTION_KEY`
stays a deployment secret because the database cannot protect its own key.

| Piece | Where | What it owns |
|---|---|---|
| Table `name_check.source_connection` | `db/schema/name-check/source-connection.ts` | One row per vendor (`euipo`, `tavily`, `brave`): `enabled`, `client_id`, `secret_ciphertext`, `api_base`, `token_url`, `version`, `updated_at/by`. Absent row = never configured. CHECKs: only EUIPO carries a client id or hosts; hosts are `https://`. |
| Reads/writes | `db/name-check/source-connections.ts` | Ciphertext in, ciphertext out. Every write is a compare-and-swap on `version`. |
| Encryption | `security/aes-gcm.ts` (`openSecret`, `KeyStatus`) + `security/encryption-key.ts` | The envelope the AI keys and Discord tokens use; `openSecret` answers none / ready / undecryptable instead of throwing. |
| Connections | `name-check/connections.ts` → `resolveNameSourceConnections(rows, key)` | Opens each secret, decides `configured` once (enabled ∧ opened ∧ for EUIPO a client id), builds the `NameSourceCredentials` the sources receive as a **closure** — the plaintext is never a field. `publicNameSourceConnection` is the only shape that crosses to a client; `security/load-leak-gate.test.ts` refuses `secretCiphertext` in any client-facing file. |
| Composition | `name-check/index.ts` → `loadNameSourceConnections()` / `loadNameSourceCredentials()` | The app-side doors: `db` + `getEncryptionKey()`, read at the start of every operation, so a save is live on the next check on every instance. The admin page uses the strict one (an unreadable table is an error it renders). The public check uses the forgiving one: an unreadable table or a rotated key becomes `credentials_missing` rows — the check never fails on its settings, and the log line names the error class, not a query. |
| Admin operations | `name-check/connection-settings.ts` | Save / remove secret / test: seal → guarded write → best-effort audit (`name_check.source.*`, detail = version, changed fields, `keyChange`; never a secret). |
| Connection test | `name-check/connection-test.ts` | The vendor's own `search()` with a fixed probe name under `SOURCE_TEST_BUDGET_MS`, one attempt, outside cache, quota and breaker, rate-limited per admin. Classified `ok / invalid_credentials / rate_limited / timeout / unavailable / unknown`; a wrong host is `unavailable`, not a wrong password, and a failure carries a secret-free `detail` naming the step and status (`token endpoint: HTTP 401` = wrong secret, `trademark search: HTTP 403` = no approved subscription yet). The EUIPO token cache is cleared first so a draft secret cannot ride the saved one's token. |

## Testing

`normalize`, `similarity`, `signal`, `relevance`, `quota` and the source **mappers** are
unit-tested with fixtures; `check.test.ts` drives the orchestrator with fake sources —
partial failure, timeout, quota, credentials, cache hit, floor, territory scoping, the
`onSourceSettled` seam, and a spy proving the name never reaches `console.error`. The HTTP
clients themselves are not mocked-and-tested: the only realistic risk there is the remote
contract, which a mock cannot witness (see `testing/strategy.md`).

## Emulating it

1. Declare each upstream as a `NameSource` — territories and `manualUrl` first, `search`
   second. A registry you cannot query still earns a row.
2. Map every thrown error class to exactly one coverage status in one place.
3. Cache successes only; put the hash of the query in the key, never the query.
4. Keep the similarity engine pure and fixture-tested; put the thresholds in `config.ts`.
5. Derive the signal from predicates over evidence, and return reasons as codes so the
   page can explain in the reader's language.
6. Rate-limit before the fan-out; quota per source; deadline per source; breaker per source.
7. Keep vendor credentials in an administrator-managed table sealed under the deployment
   key, opened once per operation into a closure — never in `.env`, never on a field.

## Later

- Progressive delivery: `checkName()` already fires `onSourceSettled` per source; an NDJSON
  route (`retrieval/ingest/stream` is the precedent) can forward rows as they land.
- Altcha escalation after repeated checks from one bucket (`verifyAltcha` exists; adaptive
  gating does not yet).
- Companies House and OpenCorporates as live sources once a key is worth its terms;
  DPMAconnectPlus if the contract is.
- A Vely tool over the same `checkName()`, saved searches, monitoring for new filings.
